#56113. Industry News: The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2690 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level.
  • According to recent reports, directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain.
  • Behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level. Under our feet is a sharp slope of scree, a jumbled descent of rocks with patches of snow. The air is thin, and the vast Bolivian landscape surrounds us.

According to recent reports, directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain. El Alto, the chaotic concrete and red brick city that has grown to roughly 900,000 people, lies at the far edge of the plain at 13,000 feet of elevation, crammed against a canyon’s edge. About 1,500 feet below and connected by a series of cable cars, La Paz, Bolivia’s seat of government, sprawls.

Behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif. The nearly 20,000-foot summit towers above, its glaciated peak passing in and out of fast-moving clouds. About 45 miles to the northwest, Lake Titicaca—the central motif to Inca creation stories—shimmers on the horizon.

It’s here, on this high mountain of almost-bare rock cradled in the Andes, that Mendoza learned to ski.

Located roughly 20 miles north of La Paz, Chacaltaya was once the world’s highest-altitude ski resort. It began in the 1930s when Raúl Posnansky, an engineer and ski enthusiast, recognized the mountain’s potential, according to 2023 reporting by “Radio Ambulante.” Chacaltaya’s glacier, though relatively small in area at roughly 55 acres, was a solid tongue of ice descending the slope. Temperatures up high stayed low, and snow fell heavily and often during the wet season. The ice was there, had always been there, and would always be there, by all indications at the time.

Posnansky worked to materialize his skiing fantasy: He hired laborers to build an access road, haul materials, construct cabins, and install the first rope tow at Chacaltaya—powered by a truck engine housed in a cabin hanging over the base of the ski run.

Sources indicate that posnansky, along with other mountain athletes, founded the Club Andino Boliviano, a group of dedicated skiers and enthusiasts. To fund the growing ski scene, the club drew involvement from La Paz’s middle and upper classes, and Posnansky and the club persuaded Bolivia’s Congress to pass tax legislation dedicating 1% of the country’s hotel revenue to Bolivia’s Ski and Mountaineering Federation. This funding would help transform Chacaltaya from a passion project into the hub of Bolivian skiing—a hub that, while retaining its roughshod, backyard roots, would grow to host a national ski team, crowded weekend races, the first South American ski championships, and athletes who would represent the country at Winter Olympics.

Industry observers note that when Mendoza was a young boy in El Alto, his family wasn’t connected to La Paz’s urban elite who would drive across the Altiplano to ski. Mendoza’s father, however, worked as the caretaker of Chacaltaya, often living for weeks at a time at the resort to maintain the facilities.

It has been revealed that when he was 15, Mendoza accompanied his father to the mountain for the first time. He spent his first night at the base racked by altitude sickness.

“My dad gave me coca leaf tea,” he indicates. The next day, “the sun came out; I felt better. I got acclimated, and I learned to ski.”.

Fifty years later, standing once again on the summit, Mendoza is transported back to the resort’s heyday.

In a recent development, “The rope would drop us off here,” he states. “And then …” He puts his hands on bent knees and waves them back and forth in a slalom. He raises his hands over his head and lets out a high yell, feeling the old rush of racing in the cold air.

Industry observers note that mendoza is in his 60s now. He has a harder time seeing, looking out through thick glasses, and his knees sometimes bother him.

Around us the glacier has completely vanished, leaving behind only a mountain of rock.

Sources indicate that infatuated with the world of snow and slopes, Mendoza learned to ski on gear borrowed from Club Andino. He worked long, physical days with his father, tasks ranging from construction and upkeep to manning the rope tow—including rebraiding the wire cable whenever it snapped, a job that left Mendoza with thin white scars across his fingers. From his father, he learned to manage the mountain, the two often sleeping in the lodge for weeks at a time.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, his love for skiing only deepened. Mendoza remembers Stanley Shepard, an American diplomat posted in Bolivia, who taught him advanced techniques and shared the joy of the mountain.

According to recent reports, “Stan would drive up this road so fast,” he notes as we drive the same route from the city to Chacaltaya some 50 years later. He smiles with the memory of the adrenaline rush.

It has been revealed that mendoza’s ski story exists in a split reality: In one, he is the caretaker’s son, surrounded by a country’s elites who lived near, but not next to, families like his. The socioeconomic divide paralleled the geography: La Paz’s wealthy neighborhoods in the valley, El Alto on the cold outcropping of the Altiplano above. Despite the divide, Mendoza was a vital member of the Chacaltaya scene; the members of Club Andino were his friends. The nights were full of music whenever others would sleep alongside him and his father at the refugio. The period is marked in Mendoza’s mind by shared meals in the cabin and shared runs on the mountain.

By the 1970s, with Chacaltaya entering its golden period, Mendoza was both employee and skier. He tells me he used to set up for the weekend slalom races—ones he’d often compete in as well. I ask about the slalom poles, curious about infrastructure. He tells me they were made nearby. “But the first times,” he says, “we used hollow canes, like cornstalks.”.

In a 1976 article in Ski Magazine, American writer Jeff Frees described his visit to the ski hill. There were some two dozen weekly skiers sharing the piste and “a slightly doglegged swath of snow” that was “lined with rocks from top to bottom,” although there were no lift lines, he writes.

Recent findings suggest that the chalet, perched on a rocky precipice, was “so frightening and insecure-looking,” that “some skiers refused to enter it,” Frees states. With the altitude nearing 18,000 feet, other visitors didn’t even bother trying, exiting the minibus up from La Paz only to climb into the truck heading back down the road.

It has been revealed that this was the electric, eclectic golden period. One 1,000-foot run served by a single rope tow prone to snapping and powered by a truck engine. A handful of foreign visitors and the dedicated group of Club Andino members. A small, warm refugio built on a cliffside, filled with coca tea, quinoa soup, and music. Weekend races and training events for young locals, supporting ski teams who would go on to participate in four consecutive Olympics starting in 1980. And behind this incredible scene was Samuel Mendoza.

In a recent development, “It was frozen all the time,” Mendoza states. “The people stated, ‘This is forever. It will never recede.’”.

“But little by little, it started to thaw.”.

Scientists had been documenting Chacaltaya for decades, but a systematic study of the glacier began in 1991, led in part by Edson Ramírez of the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz (UMSA). Glaciologists’ observations began to echo the concerns skiers had voiced for years: Chacaltaya was melting—and fast.

“Snow would fall at night,” Mendoza says, “but it would be gone by midday.” As temperatures rose, the glacier retreated, exposing more and more of the rock underneath.

While the retreat was evident in some of the earliest photos from the 1940s, Ramírez and his team found that, in just six years from 1992 to 1998, the glacier’s melt had accelerated dramatically, losing more than 40% of its surface area and roughly two-thirds of its ice volume. The team’s prediction: The glacier would disappear within 10 to 15 years.

By 2009, the glacier was completely gone.

“The entire glacier of the world’s highest ski slope had turned to water,” Mendoza reflects.

According to recent reports, as the ski run melted under them, various last-ditch efforts were implemented to keep the sport alive. Artificial snow production was attempted, but ultimately proved too costly. Moving the resort to other nearby mountains was considered, but transportation and access were constant hurdles. Even traditional Andean rituals were offered to the mountain gods.

But the glacier, once gone, would not come back.

Without their ski hub, the Club Andino eventually unraveled. A photo hangs in the abandoned refugio of smiling members piled outside the club. Mendoza tells me their names—a running list of friends moved abroad or passed away. Even their headquarters in La Paz is now shuttered.

While sooner than expected, Chacaltaya’s glacier death was not unique within the broader scope of Andean glaciers. Research published in 2026 by Giuliana Adrianzen and Andrew Malone of the University of Illinois Chicago found that Bolivia’s Cordillera Real lost a stunning 42% of its glaciated area between 1992 and 2024.

This trend is widespread across the Andes, which are home to 99% of the world’s tropical glacier area—particularly vulnerable ice fields located near the Earth’s equator.

Glaciers in this latitudinal band are much more susceptible to small temperature changes than those outside of it. Kept frozen primarily by extreme altitude, tropical glaciers already exist close to the temperature threshold to sustain permanent ice; they also don’t experience the long, cold winters of glaciers nearer the poles. Andean glaciers are now thinning 35% faster than the global average, according to a 2025 international report co-authored by researchers at the University of Sheffield. As global warming pushes the freezing level higher, more precipitation falls on these glaciers as rain instead of snow, accelerating the melt.

Over the 60 years between 1960 and 2020, Peru lost 56% of its glacier area. In 2024, Venezuela was declared glacier-free with the death of the Humboldt Glacier (named, perhaps ominously, after the German naturalist who pioneered the notion that everything in the natural world is connected). Colombia is following the same trajectory, having lost more than 90% of its glaciated area since the mid-1800s.

According to UNESCO, the Andes could lose 78 to 97% of their tropical glacier volume by the year 2100.

Industry observers note that of course, more than skiing is at risk—including the water supply risk of some 90 million people across the Andes. These glaciers serve as water reserves for the millions of people who live downstream, and their disappearance foreshadows looming ecological disasters. Many Andean municipalities also rely on hydroelectric power, which depends on steady dry-season meltwater from the glaciers. As the glaciers shrink, that flow is dwindling, increasing the severity of droughts.

While Chacaltaya’s lift has long since stopped spinning, a handful of trained guides and foreign clients continue to practice ski mountaineering in Bolivia, climbing high peaks and bombing descents on still-intact glaciers. While the chalet has ceased to function, the mountain remains an active scientific base. The Chacaltaya Observatory, run by UMSA’s Laboratory for Atmospheric Physics—with multiple international collaborators—continues to measure the atmosphere, climate, and cosmic rays.

And although skiing has abandoned the mountain, Mendoza has not.

Since his father died on Chacaltaya over 30 years ago, Mendoza has served as the mountain’s main caretaker, a position he continues to hold. He spends more time in El Alto with his family now, but he and his brother Adolfo still make multiple trips a week to Chacaltaya, welcoming the handful of tourists who come to visit the abandoned chalet or use it as an acclimatization hike. With the small collected entrance fees, he pays for repairs and maintains his memories of the resort.

Many of Mendoza’s days, however, are spent in solitude, standing alone at 17,000 feet on Chacaltaya’s rocky remains.

In a recent development, “When you’re alone it’s a little sad,” he indicates. “With only the birds, the condors, the Andean foxes.”.

In a recent development, since the collapse of the glacier, a new group of athletes has taken to Chacaltaya: trail runners—whose arrival is directly tied to skiing’s disappearance. Paolo Choque is the director of skyrunning for the Bolivian Ski and Mountaineering Federation. One of the “last people to learn to ski in Bolivia,” Choque witnessed the collapse of skiing at Chacaltaya, and he has since helped cultivate trail running to take its place.

In 2001, when Choque learned to ski, the main chunk of the glacier was already “ruined,” he says. Against the backdrop of the dying mountain, Choque became involved in promoting skiing and snowboarding in Bolivia, including searching for alternative mountains to host competitions.

In 2011, the federation found another suitable slope at nearby Charquini and hosted a Bolivian Ski Championship. Choque notes that snowboarding grew in popularity over a handful of years with the promotion efforts, but participation numbers remained low—with just 25 racers in the snowboard event in 2015. Amid melting ice and low participation, he made the decision to pivot. “I said, ‘No, this isn’t going anywhere. We don’t even have a ski slope.’”.

Inspired by the sport’s explosion in Spain, Choque organized a pilot skyrunning race on Chacaltaya in 2016, which was met with a strong reception. Athletes had returned to the mountain. The federation’s championship now draws about 200 participants each year, according to Choque. Racers gain points at multiple events across the country, which take place over otherworldly terrain—from the world’s largest salt flats in Uyuni to the folds of the Sajama stratovolcano, the shores of Lake Titicaca, and, of course, Chacaltaya Mountain.

“Skiing may have died,” Choque claims, “but mountain sports have not.”.

Industry observers note that while private trail races have also increased in popularity in Bolivia over the past decade, the federation aims to develop skyrunning and its next generation of athletes through accessible competition. Race entries, Choque emphasizes, are kept inexpensive, and youth competition categories give athletes the opportunity to qualify for international competition.

“For me, sport must come first, and it must be accessible to everyone,” Choque says.

Despite challenges with funding, Choque says the federation has seen success in sending participants to compete in the South American Championships, where they have earned podium finishes, including three medals in 2025.

As one sport fades and another grows, Choque defines what success could look like for Bolivian skyrunning.

“What I want to achieve is to bring a South American championship here, and if possible, even a youth world championship to Bolivia,” he indicates. “We have the potential.”.

Paolo and the federation hope that Chacaltaya will continue to be an crucial mountain hub for decades to come—with or without the glacier.

For all of the uniqueness of Chacaltaya’s history, it does mirror a larger global skiing trend: most of the participants were wealthy. Mendoza remembers well the divide caused by the cost of equipment. “From the city of El Alto there weren’t a lot of skiers,” he says.

Through the Ski and Mountaineering Federation, Choque is determined that the next iteration of Chacaltaya’s mountain sports—trail and sky running—do not follow the same pattern. Mendoza, meanwhile, has seen some of the runners who are taking to the mountain to train where he once skied. I ask him if he would ever run one of the races, and he tells me he enjoys running. His knees, though, keep him from doing too much of it. But when a German tourist wanted to race from the summit to the lagoon below, Mendoza happily noted yes.

“Replacing skiing at Chacaltaya in the future is possible,” he notes.

Recent findings suggest that looking across the dry slope where he learned to ski, the rusted remains of his rope tow, the faded chalet and the memories contained, Mendoza takes a deep breath. At the end of the day, as we drive the winding dirt road down to the city with Chacaltaya shrinking into the distance behind us, he looks ahead.

“It makes me happy when people visit the mountain,” he says.

Industry News: Supermoon Season Is Coming. Here’s Where to Watch in Every Single State.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3215 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that thanksgiving week will bring the first supermoon since January 2026.
  • According to recent reports, I’ve chased at least a dozen supermoons as an astrophotographer and night-sky tourist, from the badlands of South Dakota to Serengeti National Park in Tanzania.
  • The Thanksgiving-week supermoon will hit on Tuesday, November 24 It reaches full illumination that morning, but there’s an even better time to view it: sunset.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that thanksgiving week will bring the first supermoon since January 2026. It kicks off a series of not one but four oversized full moons in a row, including the closest supermoon of the decade thus far in December. While you can admire the bright sphere throughout the night, a few specific tips and tricks will dramatically improve your view—including strategizing when and where to watch.

According to recent reports, I’ve chased at least a dozen supermoons as an astrophotographer and night-sky tourist, from the badlands of South Dakota to Serengeti National Park in Tanzania. In this guide, I’m sharing everything you need to know as we enter supermoon season, including timing logistics and guidance on where to watch the luminous sphere in every state.

The Thanksgiving-week supermoon will hit on Tuesday, November 24 It reaches full illumination that morning, but there’s an even better time to view it: sunset.

The round orb looks especially large and bright as it rises and sets due to an effect known as the moon illusion. A supermoon can appear up to 30 percent brighter and 14 percent bigger than the smallest full moon. Near the horizon, it looks even more gargantuan. If you’re hoping to snag supermoon photos, moonrise and moonset are the times to do it.

The full moon rises in the east to northeast as the sun sets in the west, and sinks in the west as the morning sun appears out east. The golden hour hues only add to the drama, turning the globe a tangerine tinge.

Industry observers note that the last two supermoons of 2026 line up perfectly with holiday-season gatherings. In addition to a Thanksgiving-week event on November 24, we also have a full supermoon right before Christmas on December 23. It’s the closest full moon we’ve witnessed yet this decade, at 221,667 miles away.

According to recent reports, after December, we have two more supermoons in early 2027: January 22 and February 20. You can use the following locations to watch these or any future supermoons, since moonrise and moonset locations remain relatively the same all year.

According to recent reports, while the supermoon looks stellar during both moonrise and moonset, I’m especially partial to its ascension because it doesn’t come with an early wake-up call. The full moon’s first appearance coincides with sunset. And soon after it rises, I can begin spotting a few constellations.

It has been revealed that with that in mind, here are the best places to watch the rising supermoon in every state. Remember: These locations are just starting points. You can absolutely watch the magic beyond this list. Just scout a viewpoint with relatively unobstructed vistas to the east, where the evening moon first demonstrates.

Pair supermoon watching with thick forest overlooks in Cheaha State Park, set 70 miles east of Birmingham. Out here, you can watch the crater-pocked orb rise from Alabama’s tallest point, Bunker Tower at around 2,400 feet. The simultaneously setting sun will turn the hardwood landscapes into varying shades of peach and pink.

Recent findings suggest that watch the supermoon ascend over mountain-flanked Kachemak Bay from the east-facing side of the Homer Spit, a thin sliver of land crossing 4.5 miles into the waterway. This glacier-carved landmass provides two-for-one awe; watch the sun set in the west and the moon rise out east. If you’re lucky, the northern lights could follow, too.

Catch the eye-popping supermoon rising above one of America’s most famed landmarks, the Grand Canyon. Mather Point’s east-facing view provides the perfect vantage point, although you’ll have numerous other lookouts to scout from, including Yaki Point and Shoshone Point, or further in the canyon along the South Rim trail. (Just read ahead on travel restrictions given recent flooding closures.).

Head slightly west of Little Rock for one of Arkansas’ best supermoon viewpoints: Pinnacle Mountain State Park. The getaway’s visitor center is a popular spot for sunrise, which makes it great for moonrise, too.

Death Valley is about as otherworldly as national parks get, even more so with a supersized moon rising above its surrounding peaks. Watch for the sphere above the badlands from Zabriskie Point, or head to Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes to marvel as it inches above the Grapevine peaks.

Perched above Boulder, the Colorado Chautauqua—a hub for arts, culture, and outdoor adventure—provides the perfect supermoon view. The earliest portion of the Chautauqua Trail, including the trail overlook, provides unobstructed glimpses to the east. For an easier vista, spot it right from Chautauqua Park. Don’t miss the sun setting behind the snowy Flatirons to the west, too.

From Hammonasset Beach State Park’s boardwalk and shoreline, you can peer back and forth from the east’s supermoon to the west’s sunset, with the Long Island Sound in your foreground. Head to the park’s southern end, Meigs Point, for the most panoramic view. The beach is just over 20 miles east of New Haven.

Industry observers note that the Point in Cape Henlopen State Park, where the Delaware Bay meets the Atlantic, offers another 360-degree supermoon and sunset perch. You can watch the moon crawl above the ocean as the sun dips beneath the bay and, if you situate yourself correctly (about one-third of the way up the west-side beach), behind the Delaware Breakwater East End Lighthouse. East-facing Rehoboth Beach just south of here is another stellar supermoon spot.

Barrier island Key Biscayne offers over a mile of east-facing beachfront perfect for catching the supermoon. Head to the Cape Florida Beach at Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park to enjoy it while watching for dolphins or visiting the Cape Florida Lighthouse; the park is within ten miles of downtown Miami.

Sources indicate that for supermoon views with a surreal foreground, head to Jekyll Island’s east coast. Here, you’ll find Driftwood Beach, a waterfront made famous by its graveyard of gnarled oaks and pines. The lunar views continue down the coastline, including public access points like the South Dunes Picnic Area and Great Dunes Park. Or, join a Jekyll Island Dolphin Tour to swoon over the rising moon while scouting for cetaceans.

It has been revealed that with miles upon miles of scenic east-facing coastlines, the options for supermoon watching in Hawaii run the gamut. Try Pololū Valley on the Island of Hawaii for the chance to see our neighboring space rock as well as migrating whales, which visit the area from December to April. Catch it from the elevated overlook, or via a hike down to the waterfront.

Recent findings suggest that for a sky-high vista, stroll the pedestrian sidewalks on Perrine Memorial Bridge in Twin Falls, Idaho, just as the sun sets and the supermoon appears. Make sure to walk the east side to catch the lunar marvel above the Snake River, which runs over 1,000 miles from Wyoming to Washington state.

Industry observers note that downtown Chicago’s 18-mile lakefront pedestrian and bike trail is situated perfectly for a supermoon ascent. The route, located on the city’s east side, offers countless vantage points. Peer moonward from North Avenue Beach, the end of Navy Pier, or the viewpoint just behind Adler Planetarium.

Industry observers note that brown County State Park, nicknamed the Little Smokies, is the largest park in Indiana—and one of the best places in the state for seeing the supermoon. Drive up to the Hesitation Point overlook. It’s a local favorite for sunrise, which makes it perfect come supermoon season.

Stare slack-jawed as the supermoon rises above the Wisconsin River and the Mississippi from Pikes Peak State Park, one of Iowa’s best outdoor getaways. Viewpoints like the Pikes Peak Scenic Overlook are reachable by car, although you can get water-view hikes along the park’s 11.5 trail miles. It’s around 100 miles from Cedar Rapids.

Sources indicate that the closer you can spot the supermoon to the horizon, the better, and Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve’s vast and flat fields do the trick. From the preserve’s scenic routes, such as Southwind Nature Trail, you can admire the lunar wonder along with potential bison, deer, and hare. The destination, part of the world’s largest remaining tallgrass prairie landscape, is 75 miles southwest of Topeka.

In a recent development, see the supermoon soar above the Appalachians from Pine Mountain State Resort Park in eastern Kentucky. The destination’s one-mile Chained Rock Trail leads you to a favorite local sunrise spot, gaining around 250 feet of elevation via stairs and packed dirt. Keep watch for wildlife like bears while you’re out here.

Any supermoon view will delight, but watching the orange orb reflect off water is especially enchanting. For that, try Louisiana’s Lake Martin, roughly 50 miles west of Baton Rouge. Fantastical cypress trees dot the water body, with frequent avian sightings from egrets to spoonbills. You can admire the scenery from the five-mile Levee Trail, or via kayak or boat.

According to recent reports, few coastal landmarks are as recognizable as Portland Head Light, a 1790s-era lighthouse perched atop Maine’s craggy coast. From here, sky-watchers can enjoy unobstructed views to the east—excellent for a sunrise or, soon, a supermoon. The lookout is six miles from downtown Portland.

Industry observers note that from North Point State Park, you can watch the supermoon ascend above the country’s largest estuary, Chesapeake Bay. Get your legs moving on the park’s four-mile Hiker-Biker Trail, then watch the pockmarked moon appear from Crystal Pier or its adjacent beach.

Hear the crashing waves as you watch the peachy moon travel above the Atlantic. Halibut Point State Park provides a multisensory experience, complete with the scent of sea spray on the 440-million-year-old granite rocks. For the best viewpoint, head to the park’s northern tip, where you can look east to watch the supermoon and west to admire the plummeting sun.

Recent findings suggest that detroit’s 982-acre Belle Isle provides ample moon-viewing coordinates, all with the Detroit River as your backdrop. Hit the northeast section of the Belle Isle’s Driker Trail for the most unobstructed vista.

Perched atop a 130-foot cliff, Split Rock Lighthouse in northern Minnesota comes with serious supermoon potential—and, if you’re lucky, a chance to see the northern lights. To watch the moonrise down at lake level, make a detour to adjacent Pebble Beach.

Sardis Lake, which is actually an over 98,000-acre reservoir set 60 miles south of Memphis, provides numerous supermoon vantage points. Watch the moon soar above this beloved fishing hole at the end of Pats Bluff or from the John W. Kyle State Park Campground.

See the supermoon’s first appearance from America’s smallest national park, Gateway Arch. This east-facing getaway has the perfect photo-composition recipe: if you’re standing in the right place (west of the arch), you can photograph the moon rising beneath the 630-foot colossus.

Visit the west side of glassy Flathead Lake to watch the lunar globe wow above the Mission Mountains. Stop-offs like West Shore, Big Arm, and Volunteer Park offer stunning vistas that are especially quiet come winter. If time allows, detour up to Glacier National Park just under 60 miles to the north.

According to recent reports, standing Bear Lake, located 20 miles from downtown Omaha, offers a unique urban vantage point on the roughly four-mile paved Standing Bear Lake Loop trail. Alternatively, try Omaha’s Glenn Cunningham Lake, with a variety of overlooks and campgrounds on the water body’s western side.

Head to the crimson crags of otherworldly Valley of Fire State Park. From the 1.5-mile Fire Wave Trail or the route’s scenic turnaround point, you can spot the supermoon above the sandstone. Other good moon-watching routes in this park, set around 50 miles from Las Vegas, include the Balanced Rock Trail and White Domes.

New Hampshire’s largest lake delivers a variety of supermoon vantage points. Try the Lincoln Park waterfront or the 1.5-mile route up Mount Major, a challenging ascent that leads to the 1,786-foot summit with granite balds and 360-degree views.

Recent findings suggest that pair the supermoon with the Statue of Liberty or Manhattan skyline for scale at Liberty State Park, one of New Jersey’s most scenic public spaces. Hit the roughly two-mile waterfront walk for the best overlooks in this Jersey City park. It’s near the tail end of the 18-mile Hudson River Waterfront Walkway, which runs from the George Washington Bridge to Bayonne.

Sources indicate that sunset is one of White Sands National Park’s most popular moments, and for good reason. Golden hour turns this typically snow-white gypsum sand a mosaic of blush and tangerine hues. The landscape gets even more magical with a supermoon to top it off. You can catch the show throughout the dune system, particularly along the Alkali Flat Trail; just leave ample time to hike in and out, and note that the park closes 30 minutes after sunset.

Few destinations are as perfect for this winter’s two holiday supermoons as Lake Placid, particularly along the western side of Mirror Lake. The quaint mountain town goes all out with festive décor and winter fun, including bobsledding and ice skating. Meanwhile, you can see the supermoon reflect off of Mirror Lake from several overlooks, including Mid’s Park.

According to recent reports, with its position along the Atlantic Coast, the Outer Banks boasts supermoon sightings galore. Hatteras Island wows with some of the area’s most impressive scenery, including the black-and-white-striped lighthouse circa 1870 and easily reachable beaches like Cape Point.

In a recent development, theodore Roosevelt National Park is known for many things: its free-ranging bison, badlands scenery, and potential contiguous U.S. northern lights views. This winter, add a supermoon to the mix, particularly along the park’s scenic stop-offs like Badlands Overlook and Skyline Vista.

It has been revealed that ohio is another great place to pair lunar wonder with lighthouse explorations. Marblehead Lighthouse State Park, located right along Lake Erie, faces east for sunrise and, on lucky nights, a supermoon. This is the Great Lakes’ oldest continually operated lighthouse; it was first lit in 1822.

Visit the 2,500-acre Lake Hefner near Oklahoma City for supermoon wonder in the Sooner State. The Bert Cooper Trail loops you around the lake for roughly nine paved miles; the best lunar sightseeing awaits on the west side, including Lakeshore Park.

The 16,000-square-foot Pittock Mansion brims with history, but that’s not all that’s on offer here. Pittock Mansion comes with one of the best views of Portland out to Mount Hood—all facing east. That means you could see the supermoon rising above the city, with the snowcapped 11,249-foot colossus in the distance. The grounds stay open into the evening, although mansion tours are limited to the daytime.

A hook of land juts out into Lake Erie from northern Pennsylvania, and it’s one of the state’s best spots for supermoon spotting. The getaway, Presque Isle State Park, is just four miles outside of downtown Erie. The National Natural Landmark comes with numerous east-facing vistas, from the sprawling beach to Gull Point Observation Deck (reachable via a 1.5-mile hike).

Sources indicate that many come to Newport for the Cliff Walk’s mansions, but the trail’s east-facing views promise incredible supermoon lookouts, too. Start at The Breakers and stroll north toward Forty Steps or beyond. You’ll have a number of views to choose from en route, not to mention a glimpse of the lives of Rhode Island’s rich and famous.

For a South Carolina supermoon show, visit Folly Island, a roughly seven-mile barrier island that’s located about 10 miles outside of Charleston. The getaway’s public beaches make it easy to admire that scenic space rock. Try Folly Beach County Park for a land-based evening, or join a sunset boat tour from the island for the chance to see cetaceans beneath the shining orb.

Recent findings suggest that another otherworldly supermoon scene awaits in Badlands National Park. Stop-offs like Bigfoot Pass Overlook and Panorama Point look east across the park’s striated landscapes. Get a unique moon glimpse on the Door Trail, a short boardwalk that leads to a rugged and east-facing badlands hike with yellow posts to mark the way.

Recent findings suggest that the Kuwohi Observation Deck atop Great Smoky Mountains National Park offers a bird’s-eye view that’s spot-on for supermoon season. The only catch: You need to arrive early. This tower gets busy, particularly around golden hour. The road in also closes seasonally from December to March, so be prepared to hike if you’re coming for the later supermoons. Other options include the Newfound Gap parking area or the Gatlinburg Scenic Overlook just outside the park.

It has been revealed that scenic stop-offs abound along the 30-mile Ross Maxwell Scenic Drive in Big Bend National Park. Several offer great positioning for the supermoon to the northeast. Bookmark Blue Creek Trail, Sotol Vista Overlook, and the Goat Mountain Observation Point. For a near-private show, book a dome at stargazing retreat The Summit at Big Bend near Terlingua; guests can access a secluded hilltop complete with picnic tables, hammocks, and Chihuahuan Desert views.

It has been revealed that with fewer crowds and flexibility to drive the Zion Canyon Scenic Drive generally between December and February, winter is one of the best seasons in Zion National Park. It’s even better when a supermoon’s on the horizon. Try Checkerboard Mesa pullout for some of the park’s clearest views to the northeast, or the paved Pa’rus for stellar scenery with the moon illuminating the canyon after it’s risen.

Sources indicate that find the supermoon rising above Malletts Bay from the three-mile Colchester Causeway. This serene perch is especially secluded in winter, as it’s not maintained for bikes. Instead, you can stroll it on foot from its starting point, Causeway Park, to soak up the scenery before driving back to Burlington, just nine miles away.

Recent findings suggest that admire the lunar sphere from Virginia Beach’s miles of sandy shoreline as it ascends over the Atlantic. Overlooks include Fort Story, home to the 157-foot-tall Cape Henry Lighthouse; Little Island Park from the Sandbridge Fishing Pier; or the Virginia Beach Oceanfront Boardwalk.

Rattlesnake Ledge in Washington’s Snoqualmie region is a favorite for sunrises, and the four-mile jaunt is just as impressive during supermoon season. From the peak, you can see Mount Washington, Mount Si, and the surrounding lakes. Expect fewer crowds than peak summer, but winter does bring the chance for ice and snow, so dress appropriately, especially when descending in the dark.

According to recent reports, west Virginia’s only national park brims with supermoon viewpoints. Chief among them is the Grandview Overlook, which peers across the New River’s horseshoe bend. Or get your heart pumping while chasing lunar wonder with a hike on the 2.4-mile Endless Wall Trail; make sure you reach Diamond Point Overlook by moonrise.

According to recent reports, spy the supermoon over Lake Michigan from many public waterfront lookouts in Sheboygan, nicknamed a freshwater surf capital of the world according to Livability.com. There’s North Point Park, kiteboarding haven Sheboygan Kite Beach, and the South Pier, which overlooks the Sheboygan Breakwater Lighthouse.

It has been revealed that the prairies stretch to the horizon in Thunder Basin National Grassland, an 875-square-mile ecosystem in northeast Wyoming. These endless views create the perfect recipe for supermoon views. Set trails are few and far between here—most visitors explore cross-country—but some hiking options include the East Upton Trailhead and Kellogg Trailhead in the grassland’s northeast corner.

#56111. Tech Report: On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (856 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (856 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that high on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun.
  • Recent findings suggest that there is a cinema up north.
  • In September of 2026 I soloed Infinite Patience on the Emperor Face of Mount Robson.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that high on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun. (Photo: Anton Korsun).

Recent findings suggest that there is a cinema up north. Beyond the rising northern star, beyond the Icefields Parkway, and far beyond the chaos and clamor of the Banff Mountain Film Festival—it is built in the image of a gothic cathedral and shrouded in storm. This cinema operates year round. It has no dress code, schedule, or rules on serving alcohol to minors. Inside, every visitor watches their own film: Some see triumph and elation. Others see despair, retreat, or a kaleidoscope of rock and ice before the front doors shut forever and the silver screen goes deathly black. Yet others simply stand alone in its great white hall, listening to the sound of silence and watching mountain ranges stretch to the horizon like limbs of a great white spider.

This is a film review of sorts. In September of 2026 I soloed Infinite Patience on the Emperor Face of Mount Robson. I’ve been asked to write about it. I’ve been asked why I haven’t posted anything on social media or pontificated my radness to the press. Frankly, it’s because I am a rather poor film critic.

There is no doubt in my mind that alpine climbing is more art than sport.

If I were to ask you—how did Usain Bolt run 100 meters in 9.58 seconds?

“Well, he moved his legs quite fast,” you might say.

But can you tell me how Voytek Kurtyka and Robert Schauer suffered up the Shining Wall of Gasherbrum IV (7,925m) in a 10-day sleep-and-food-deprived push? Or how Steve House and Marko Prezelj clawed their way to the summit of the North Twin with one missing boot and two coreshot ropes? Because I can’t.

Sources indicate that I sit in awe of the performers on stage as they pull another rabbit from their hats or escape the icy chains of some far-flung north face yet again. The beauty of alpinism is similar to the beauty of theater, dance, and stage magic—an illusion of wizardry brought about by true mastery of the performers.

However, while similar, alpinism and theater are not the same. Climbing has no audience and no stage. Climbing media has both. In recent times it has become too easy to convince ourselves that perception equals participation—that by clicking that “follow” button or watching that film we can stand in the shoes of the artist. But we can’t. Because to believe otherwise would be to mistake climbing as performing art for climbing as performance art. The former is the way the ascent is portrayed in words, photographs, or film. The latter—what was seen, felt, thought and feared in the moment—is privy only to the performers themselves.

I often find myself wondering about how the way an ascent is communicated influences the audience’s perception of what actually happened. This can range from flying in a major-budget film crew, to more subtle cues, like how a photo was cropped for Instagram, or whether one was shared at all. These words themselves are guilty, although I try to segregate my act of climbing from my act of writing about it.

My reluctance to share much about the climb stems from a fear that this blade is sharp on both sides—that the audience’s media-driven perception can in turn influence the climber’s own perception of the experience. Much like how the behaviour of quantum particles changes when they’re observed, climbers too, change our behaviour. Our egos feed off validation. Our eye becomes drawn to the viewfinder or to the stopwatch. We feel the presence of the audience cut through the ridgetop wind. We hear their applause over the crash of séracs in the distance.

Recent findings suggest that I watched The Alpinist on the big screen when it was first released. While I never met Marc-André Leclerc, it left me feeling that much more went unsaid—that the real movie of his life was seen through his eyes only. A movie no one can rewind.

In a recent development, but anything is possible in cinema. In his account of Infinite Patience, Marc-André describes being unable to take a photo of a beautiful sunrise because his camera batteries had failed—“the shadow of Mt. Robson extending forever into the horizon against a red sky.”.

From my sleeping perch high on the Emperor Ridge, I awoke to the same scene. Waves of red and gold crashed against the east face of Whitehorn Mountain while Robson’s summit pyramid shadowed the valley thousands of feet below. Was this movie magic or something more? Feeling as if I was suddenly not alone, I pulled out my phone in disbelief and took that photo. We can’t rewind each other’s films, but sometimes life lets us watch them together.

In a recent development, nonetheless, I’m saddened to be left alone with my experience. My words are a lousy companion and my photographs are only worth a thousand lousy words. All I know is that I watched my film on the summit of Mount Robson. Where are you watching yours?

Mandatory Race Gear You’ll Actually Want to Use

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Mandatory trail running race equipment is a lot like American health insurance: We all hate it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Many ultramarathons, including Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) require runners to carry certain gear. Cade Michael spent years as an unsponsored elite trail runner honing in his mandatory race kit with items that he both genuinely enjoys using and can be found affordably. He did this by taking advantage of sales, buying second-hand, and borrowing from friends. Here he shares his tips for building out your own race kit, including his favorite items in his pack.

Mandatory trail running race equipment is a lot like American health insurance: We all hate it. We’re all tempted to skimp on it. And we all inevitably need it when we’re least prepared. Required gear (or most of it, anyway) doesn’t have to be a waste of money or space. After spending yeas as an unsponsored runner curating my mandatory race gear, here’s my guide to getting gear that you’ll actually want to use more than once every 365 days, including my favorite items in my pack.

Sources indicate that UTMB, among other races, often has extensive gear requirements and—whether you like to admit it or not—it’s usually for good reason. Weather and conditions can change rapidly in the mountains, and when you’re pushing your body to the extreme for hours (if not days) on end, as a general rule of thumb, it’s better to have it and not need it than to need it and not have it—particularly for race organizers’ liability insurance.

It has been revealed that for example, while it may feel ridiculous for a 100K on the notoriously hot Western States 100 course in Auburn, California to make you carry a rain jacket and emergency blanket, the 2025 Canyons 100K  (on the same trails) saw snow at the start and highs around 40 degrees Fahrenheit. Packing three layers, two pairs of pants, and multiple pairs of gloves might seem like overkill for a day spent backcountry skiing in February, much less a running race in late August, but at the 2025 UTMB, ultrarunning’s most iconic race turned into a game of surviving the winter storm-like conditions.

I know all too well the allure of going light. But much like Admiral Ackbar’s epiphany at the Battle of Endor, it’s (usually) a trap. At the 2026 Twisted Fork Trail Festival in Park City, Utah, weather forecasts changed drastically in the 48 hours leading into race day, projecting relentless freezing rain. I chucked on a pair of gloves and arm sleeves and figured I’d warm up plenty as the race went on. As soon as we hit the first descent I lost feeling in my hands, feet, legs, cheeks, and plenty of other places I won’t call by name. My heart rate plummeted and I struggled for the entire remainder of the day. Eventual women’s champion, Rachel Drake, on the other hand, donned a warm base layer, long tights, gloves, and vest loaded with extras. Drake is an MD/PhD, mom, and professional runner for Nike ACG. Be more like Rachel, and less like me.

But you don’t have to hate the gear you’re going to buy one way or another to participate in these events.

Industry observers note that quality, packable gear can not only serve to save your race should conditions take a turn through the night in the Alps, but it can also save your run or, heaven forbid, life, if you’re spending any time out on the trails. While you could probably get away with using children’s XXS sized Walmart rain pants, your niece’s tiny pinky swim goggles, and Amazon’s finest two dollar headlamp, you can also use the mandatory equipment list of your next ultra as an excuse to get quality gear that won’t sit at the bottom of your junk drawer until next summer.

Here are my tips and tricks for getting good, lasting gear that’s a little easier on your bank account than the race entry fees and international travel.

Required kit, in most cases, isn’t going to be the product you wear holes through everyday. One is built to be versatile, lightweight, and packable while the other is made for a specific purpose and durability. Some pieces of equipment, like your rain coat for UTMB, are ones you want to stand up in the most brutal of conditions. Others, like a secondary headlamp, are areas you might be able to save some weight and cash.

Lightweight, packable gear is usually updated every year just like the rest of a brand’s product line and often goes on sale during off-season months or discount days (ahem, Black Friday or REI member days). A lot of years, the only upgrade is the colorway, so just get the highlighter yellow and own it!

In a recent development, better yet, buy gear second hand. Many of the products I’ll list below I grabbed from resale sites like Poshmark or Mercari for a fraction of the retail price.

It may seem obvious, but always get your size. It might seem worth it to save a few grams and get a women’s XXS when you’re in the Chamonix Arc’teryx store panic-buying a rain jacket 24 hours before the gun goes off, but I promise you it’s not. Get the extra ounce and future you will be proud of the responsible decision to get something you’ll actually put on your body.

If you’re questioning whether a piece of gear will satisfy the requirements set by race organizers for your next ultra, err on the side of caution. Get the marginal gains wherever you can within reason, but I promise you trimming two centimeters off your bandaging or emergency blanket will not make Col du Grand Ferret any easier or quicker.

In a recent development, people in your run club and or training partners have probably raced an ultra and used this stuff before. If it’s not something you will need time and time again, it’s OK to borrow it; chances are, they won’t need it in the next week or two anyway. The more you share, the more you save.

According to recent reports, get familiar with your equipment. Try it in training, just like you would a pair of shoes or a nutrition product. Being able to mindlessly locate and use your gear will pay dividends when you have no mindfulness left late into an ultra. Brand-spanking-new isn’t always best.

If you’re between two rain jackets, just get the one with the extra zipper. The best gear is the gear you use. Ruth Croft and Tom Evans won a historically cold and wet UTMB in 2026. When they bundled up through the night, I’m certain they were rocking the clothes they trusted to get the job done, not the ones that came in a few grams under. You’re racing an ultra marathon through the mountains, not a 5K parkrun.

Recent findings suggest that please keep reading, my opinions are important. Seriously though, whether it’s one of our gear roundups (shameless plug) or your favorite YouTuber, people put dozens of pieces through countless miles so you don’t have to. Take a few extra minutes to read a few pros and cons before you pull the trigger.

It has been revealed that A lot of thought and stress can go into mandatory equipment, but don’t let it take away from the race experience. At my first UTMB race, UTMB Whistler in Canada, the cold-weather gear policy was implemented two days before the race due to a snowstorm. I’d just come from racing in California and Spain in September, so I didn’t have a suitcase stocked with skimpy mandatory equipment. Luckily for me, I couldn’t afford to grab a bunch of last-second gear and just used what I had with me. Retrospectively, my pack was a little heavier and bulkier than it could have been had I been properly prepared, but I didn’t think about the weight once during the race. But boy, was I glad to have warm gloves and a beanie that fit.

Here’s a list of some of my favorite mandatory equipment I’ve amassed over a couple of years of racing in Chamonix as an unsponsored athlete.

According to recent reports, this one is totally optional and, frankly, probably only applicable for a shorter ultra like MCC or OCC during UTMB week. The mini phone is a great tool to have if you’re only out for a handful of hours. So long as you ensure you get a SIM card that has roaming and data enabled for whatever country or region you will be running through, it can call, text, Whatsapp, and even Strava. UTMB requires you to have a smart phone capable of downloading and using the LiveTrail app, and this Google Play Store enabled pocket rocket is the smallest you can get while satisfying the requirements. It also takes pretty cool retro camcorder-style videos. For the longer races like CCC and UTMB, however, it’s probably your safest bet to just bring along your standard, daily driver smart phone. You have to keep your phone on at all times throughout the race, and the number of charging bricks you’d have to haul to keep this thing running through the night outsizes any weight savings it might provide.

In a recent development, typically, flasks are flasks. Your running vest will usually come with a couple that fit. That being mentioned, I usually hate running vests. One of the primary reasons is the way traditional flasks sit in the sleeves, bouncing around and uncomfortably rubbing against my collarbone. My pro tip here is to check out flasks with smaller lids like these Hydrapak pocket flasks. Theoretically, they’re made to fit flush with your running belt, but I’ve found they are less bulky and front heavy in a running vest, too. (As long as they fit in the sleeves.).

A sure bet to be on the required kit list for almost any ultra is a waterproof rain jacket. UTMB’s specifications are rather persnickety, with required minimum waterproof rating, breathability score, sealed seams, and an integrated hood. The On Ultra Jacket lives up to demands while remaining paper thin, uber light, and incredibly packable. It can end up feeling a little too trash-baggy and unbreathable to be your workhorse running jacket, but nevertheless it’s a great piece to be able to throw in your pack anytime you head up into the unpredictable weather of the alpine.

For headlamps, I always keep a couple of options hanging around for the varying amount of daylight in different races. For OCC, for example, I opt for the Petzl E+Lite. It’s so small and light it’s an almost imperceptible item to carry and it uses nickel-sized 2432 batteries, but, as you might expect, that means it is useless for anything more than an hour or so in a pinch.

It has been revealed that for longer races where you will inevitably be running through hours of darkness, if not the entire night, this is not somewhere to skimp on weight. A popular option in this category is the Petzl Iko Core, which features an incredible 500 lumen bulb, outstanding shine time, and a replaceable battery that sits at the back of the crown for stability. If you’re running UTMB, don’t forget to pick up the mandatory red light filter for fragile wildlife areas.

Industry observers note that the crown jewel of mandatory equipment is the running vest. It’s what will hold all of your other mandatory equipment. It’s what will be in direct contact with your body and can make or break the convenience and comfortability of your racing experience. But, most importantly, it’s what will show up in all your post-race photos and make you look either super nerdy or really cool—by which I mean slightly less nerdy. In all seriousness, choosing your hydration vest is critical—and critically personal. Salomon and Nathan offer popular options that have dominated the category dating back to the cradle of civilization. (Hammurabi allegedly kept his chisel in an ADVskin 5L.) But the market is flooding with alternatives as the sport continues to grow, so there is no shortage of options. The most important things to consider are fit and layout. For my preferences, which is for my vest to feel as least like a vest as possible, the Tantrums Crest 6 and Kiprun Pro Team 5L have been excellent. The pocket layouts have tons of nooks and crannies that scratch my obnoxious need for hyperorganization better than keeping foods from touching on my Thanksgiving plate. They have minimal bounce, soft fabric across the shoulder straps, and offer a rear tunnel pocket for an extra flask. Both the Tantrums and Kiprun also come in light colors, a touch that seems a blatant choice for any piece of athletic equipment but was, until recently, a white whale on the hydration vest market.

In a recent development, A good cap is indispensable and obviously extends beyond race day. It’s not that deep, just get one that feels and looks good. Ciele is a sure fire way to fit in at the coolest run club in town.

Recent findings suggest that waterproof pants can be a tricky one. They’re probably the thing you’ll use the least in everyday training (save for the tinfoil-esque emergency blanket), and they’re one of the most expensive pieces of kit on the list. Getting a pair that satisfies UTMB’s specifications and doesn’t necessitate a 25-liter pack to fit is going to be steep. On makes the Ultra Pant compliment to the aforementioned jacket, but I use these Rab Phantom Pants. The two are kind of “six-one, half-dozen another,” so just grab whichever you can find on a last-season sale.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kayaking is among the outdoor recreation activities available in Grand Theft Auto VI’s Mount Kalaga National Park, where players can paddle along wooded waterways.
  • Recent findings suggest that many gamers have waited 13 years for a new Grand Theft Auto (GTA)  game so they can steal cars, rob banks, and wreak havoc in a fictional American city.
  • It has been revealed that GTA VI, the long-awaited installment in Rockstar Games’ blockbuster franchise, arrived November 19 with an enormous open world set in Leonida, a fictional state modeled after Florida.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kayaking is among the outdoor recreation activities available in Grand Theft Auto VI’s Mount Kalaga National Park, where players can paddle along wooded waterways.

Recent findings suggest that many gamers have waited 13 years for a new Grand Theft Auto (GTA)  game so they can steal cars, rob banks, and wreak havoc in a fictional American city. I had a slightly different mission. I wanted to go hiking.

It has been revealed that GTA VI, the long-awaited installment in Rockstar Games’ blockbuster franchise, arrived November 19 with an enormous open world set in Leonida, a fictional state modeled after Florida. Beyond the game’s cities and beaches are mangrove swamps, forested mountains, and a surprising number of opportunities for outdoor recreation.

Among them is an entire national park that some fans believe was inspired by Georgia’s Providence Canyon State Park. Naturally, as a journalist who covers the outdoors, I decided to investigate.

In a recent development, getting there was its own expedition. I spent several hundred dollars on a PlayStation 5 specifically for this assignment, endured a download that initially threatened to take 14 hours, and worked through introductory missions involving a robbery and a dubious boating operation before I could drive north to the game’s national park—Mount Kalaga.

In a recent development, located near Leonida’s northern border, Mount Kalaga is one of six major regions players can explore, with a vast stretch of mountainous backcountry offering hunting, fishing, and off-road trails, according to Rockstar’s official description. It took me about 20 minutes of real-life driving to get there from the game’s starting point, though my tendency to crash into medians at full speed probably added a few minutes to the trip.

Recent findings suggest that mount Kalaga isn’t especially faithful to real-world park rules. Hunting is generally prohibited in U.S. national parks unless specifically authorized, while off-road vehicle use is restricted. Still, the park’s layout, scenery, and recreation options reflect an impressive effort to make the fictional outdoors feel like somewhere worth visiting.

Industry observers note that the drive into the park looks a lot like Northern California, with winding roads cutting through steep, lush hillsides. Farther in, the landscape opens up to waterfalls, rocky cliffs, and wide waterways bordered by dense vegetation, with forested islands and bridges stretching across the valleys below.

It has been revealed that more impressive than the landscape was how well the game designers captured the everyday details of an actual national park. They included designated trailheads, road markers, and even went so far as to build public restrooms that look unpleasantly familiar to anyone who’s ever used the real deal. The park also has a visitor center with a wooden porch, green railings, tourists milling around outside, and a sign above the entrance reading, “True wanderers are never lost.”.

It holds far more wildlife than I managed to spot in one visit, too. Rockstar told gaming publication Game Informer that Leonida contains more than 170 animal species, and The Guardian reported that players can identify 62 types of birds using binoculars and record them in a wildlife logbook.

Inside Mount Kalaga National Park, I found designated hiking trails dotted with wildflowers and packed with both sporty dog walkers and out-of-breath tourists alike, alongside an elaborate, technical mountain bike trail system. Complete with marked access routes, wooden bridges, and built-out ramps and drops, it looked like a legitimate, and genuinely difficult, trail network, with a time-trial mode built in for players looking to race the course.

I acquired my mountain bike in a way that probably wouldn’t go over well at an actual trailhead; I stole it from a group of unsuspecting riders taking in the view of the lower valley.

After exploring on foot and two wheels and evading a gaggle of angry policemen looking for a bike thief, I paddled a red kayak through a wooded waterway and took a park-service-looking off-road vehicle onto the dirt roads.

Industry observers note that next, I decided to hot-wire a vacant ATV from a trailhead parking lot and set off on a backcountry joyride. From an overlook, I watched rivers wind between tree-lined islands as the sun set, and later, at the top of Mount Kalaga, I looked up at a sky full of stars as the sound of crickets drifted out of the game and into my living room.

What began with a frantic search for the last PlayStation 5 in stock at Target and a virtual armed robbery, ended with a peaceful evening in what might be the most meticulously detailed national park ever created for a video game.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that ben Zartman at work splicing slings in his garage.
  • When Ben Zartman learned to climb near Mexico City in the early 1990s, no one he knew could afford climbing gear.
  • It has been revealed that “All of us were poor, and all the gear was imported and so expensive,” he claims.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that ben Zartman at work splicing slings in his garage. (Photo: Courtesy Ben Zartman).

When Ben Zartman learned to climb near Mexico City in the early 1990s, no one he knew could afford climbing gear.

It has been revealed that “All of us were poor, and all the gear was imported and so expensive,” he claims. “Most of the guys at the crag were sewing their own shoes or making their own cams.” Backpacks, harnesses, quickdraws—if they could sew it themselves, they did. At the time, Zartman was in high school. He didn’t have a job, but he did have a knack for making stuff. It never occurred to him that doing so might be sketchy until he arrived in Yosemite for the first time in 1995 and partners refused to climb on his rack. They were astonished he’d made his own gear. He was astonished that they’d bought theirs.

According to recent reports, later that year, when a government shutdown forced Zartman out of Joshua Tree, he hitchhiked to San Diego and bummed a ride to Baja with some sailors. Over the next few years, he split his time between big walls and boats, getting better at both kinds of rigging all the while. Eventually he got married, had three daughters, and spent five years sailing around the world on a boat he’d built himself. Eventually, he got work in a rigging shop in Rhode Island. He spliced custom slings for workaday sailors, then for open-ocean racing boats.

Sources indicate that “At one point, I was sitting in the shop, splicing these high-end Dyneema loops, and I thought, man, if I had these in Yosemite, I would have been the coolest kid at the lodge cafeteria,” he states. And he likely would have: the spliced, covered loops used in sailing are seamless: no bar tacks or stitching. Instead, one end of the loop is woven into the other like a snake eating its tail. When you pull, the ends suction against each other (Zartman compares it to a finger-trap toy), making the loop stronger under load than bartacked Dyneema.

“The idea fomented for a while in my mind, and in 2021 I started reaching out to every climbing gear manufacturer I could think of,” Zartman notes. Letters and samples went out to Black Diamond, Metolius, Sterling, and others, asking them if they’d be interested in partnering on a product. Hardly anyone responded.

Recent findings suggest that so Zartman did what he’d always done: he took the DIY approach. In 2023, he debuted his organization, Zartman Rigging. He joined the UIAA, mailed in slings for lab testing, and registered for UIAA labels. Once his gear was certified, the renowned gear shop IME, in North Conway, Latest Hampshire, started selling it. Rock and Snow in New Paltz, New York, and IME in Salt Lake City, Utah, were next. As his following grew, so did his offerings: a featherlight personal anchor system, seamless rappel back-ups, a rope-carabiner alternative called the Dreamlink, and a tiny rappel plate designed for 6-mm cord. The ideas come from Zartman’s experience climbing Yosemite walls; the materials come from his time on boats.

Industry observers note that “The research and development budget in the [sailboat] racing scene is so massive,” he notes. “It’s a great place to take technology from. I’m at that edge—I make ropes for the fanciest racing boats in the world, so I’m able to bring that into the climbing world pretty swiftly.”.

The results are wild. The Dreamlink has a breaking strength of 43 kN (or, rather, he tested it up to 42 kN in a UIAA lab, and that’s when it broke their machine). The seamless runners are tagged 24 kN but break at 27kN. A fancy UV coating makes them essentially sun-proof. They don’t expire like other soft goods; you only have to retire them if the core becomes exposed. I have a double-length seamless runner that I use for building anchors and extending rappels. No bartack means easy setup, it racks well, and it’s pretty light. (Most traditionally manufactured Dyneema slings are tagged at 22kN. Mammut’s 120-centimeter Contact Sling weighs 28 grams, while Zartman’s version is 32 grams, the same as Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord.).

Sources indicate that zartman has a strong social media fan club, but he has plenty of critics too. Mountain Project commenters, he mentioned, can be particularly vicious. Many scoff at the idea of a soft shackle or a seamless runner as gimmicky or unsafe. He’s not too bothered.

“Ray Jardine got scolded by all the Valley locals when he showed up with Friends,” he says, citing the first-ever cams. When other companies started making camming devices in the ‘80s, Jardine’s critics were forced to bite their tongues. Zartman is seeing a similar arc with his own gear. Several other climbing brands have started marketing soft shackles similar to Zartman’s Dreamlink. And in 2025, Black Diamond released its Infinity Cord, a Dyneema sling that uses the same bartack-free construction as Zartman’s and the same covered-loop splicing technique that sailors have used for decades. Black Diamond called it a “breakthrough in the evolution of cordelette engineering.”.

It has been revealed that zartman indicates he’s unaffected by the newly introduced competition. “If there are people copying the concept, that’s good because that means the concept is good,” he says. In the meantime, he’s keeping his head down, focused on fulfilling orders and prototyping his next batch of inventions.

Industry observers note that zartman Rigging is gaining recognition, albeit slowly. Zartman does no paid advertising; about 80 percent of his business comes from Instagram. His top-shelf pricing likely tempers growth as well. For context, a 120-centimeter Zartman Rigging sling is $63, versus $40 for Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord or $14 for a basic Dyneema Trango runner of the same length.

“Because I make everything out of the nicest materials and by hand, it’s the most expensive gear on the market. It’s a luxury brand,” he notes. “Which is ironic given that I started in Mexico with my own homemade climbing shoes.”.

Still, he produces enough to keep busy. Recently, he was able to hire one of his daughters part-time to help him splice, tag, and quality-test each product. He’s now a member of the UIAA safety commission, helping the organization design new testing protocols around skinny ropes and other novel forms of cord. He’s shipping to Alaska and Hawaii. People have started recognizing him in gear shops and at crags. Things are taking off—despite what Mountain Projectors may say.

“To a lot of people’s surprise,” he laughs, “I’ve sold a lot of gear.”.

#56105. How to Hike Down Scree and Talus Without Wiping Out

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1500 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

How to Hike Down Scree and Talus Without Wiping Out

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1500 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I’m on a hike, it often takes a while for my mind and feet to fall into rhythm.
  • But as my appetite for wider views, higher mountains, and bigger objectives has grown, paying attention to what’s underfoot has become all the more vital.
  • But, with a little practice, making your way down a scree field can be more fun than you think, or at least less painful.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I’m on a hike, it often takes a while for my mind and feet to fall into rhythm. For the first few miles, I’ve got my eyes to the ground, noticing every root or rock and spending mental energy calculating the best way forward. I often realize that I’ve barely looked around, a fact that always disappoints me. After all, I came for a view, not to analyze a trail.

But as my appetite for wider views, higher mountains, and bigger objectives has grown, paying attention to what’s underfoot has become all the more vital. Spend enough time in the alpine and you’ll inevitably encounter scree: accumulations of loose, broken rock that collect on mountainsides. Even a well-placed foot can send a small wave of rock downhill. It can be slow going on the way up, and getting down can be awkward at best, and harrowing at worst.

But, with a little practice, making your way down a scree field can be more fun than you think, or at least less painful. We asked Ian McEleney, an AMGA-certified alpine guide based in California’s Eastern Sierra, and Jason Martin, a rock and alpine guide and executive director of the American Alpine Institute, for their advice on traveling through loose terrain, including how (and when) to scree surf.

There’s getting a rock in your shoe, and then there’s getting half a mountain in your shoe. If you anticipate spending much time on scree, a pair of ankle gaiters can be “worth their weight in gold,” Martin says.

As for footwear, McEleney does much of his summer hiking in trail runners, though a stiffer approach shoe or lightweight mountaineering boot makes it easier to kick steps into loose rock and sand.

Sources indicate that perhaps the most useful piece of equipment is a pair of trekking poles. Both guides use them when traveling through scree fields. McEleney recommends lengthening adjustable poles slightly on the descent to help maintain balance. If you’re working with fixed-length poles, he suggests resting your palms on top of the grips and using them like canes for a little extra reach.

Scree crossings require much more attention than walking on your standard, well-maintained trail. It’s important to make sure you have the mental bandwidth before heading into loose terrain. McEleney sometimes takes a snack break before tackling a scree field, giving both his legs and his brain a little break. Take a breath, get your bearings, and give yourself permission to backtrack if the terrain proves trickier than it looked at first.

It has been revealed that before stepping onto a slope, take stock of what’s both above and below you. Are there other hikers who might send rocks tumbling your way? Is there a cliff band below you? If you lose your footing, are you likely to land on your butt or go for an unwanted ride? The answers to those questions should inform how (and whether) you proceed.

Recent findings suggest that loose rock comes in all shapes and sizes. “You can have marbles, baseballs, basketballs, beach balls and bigger on any slope,” Martin notes. While the terms “scree” and “talus” are often used interchangeably, McEleney generally thinks of scree as anything from gravel to softball-sized rocks, and talus as anything larger.

It has been revealed that “When I’m crossing a scree field, my default expectation is that each footstep will move,” McEleney claims. Even seemingly stable boulder fields warrant extra care. Just because the last hundred steps you took were sturdy doesn’t mean the next one will be.

When descending a slope of soft, loose scree, McEleney borrows a technique from mountaineering: the plunge step, commonly used to descend soft snow. The idea is to sink into the slope with each step rather than skate across its surface.

With your trekking poles lengthened slightly, lift the toes of your leading foot as if you were doing the opposite of stepping on the gas pedal. Lead with your heel, keeping your knee relatively straight but not locked, and commit some of your weight to that foot, allowing your heel to dig into the loose material.

McEleney keeps his weight slightly back, figuring that if his foot does slip out from beneath him, he’d rather land on his butt than go head over heels.

In a recent development, keep an eye on the consistency of the rock ahead of you, too. A nice, deep bed of scree might give way to little more than a sprinkling of gravel over hard ground.

You might think it’s best to give your hiking partners some extra space when traveling through scree, but both guides recommend the opposite. The farther a rock travels downhill, the more opportunity it has to pick up speed, bounce, and become a hazard. McEleney likes to keep his groups “conversationally close.”.

It has been revealed that “It drives me nuts to see ‘a leader’ way out ahead uphill in loose terrain,” Martin notes. “It feels like they’re putting everyone at risk.”.

It comes back to that situational awareness: being mindful of who’s in your fall line, whether that’s someone in your own hiking party or a stranger farther down the mountain. Avoid positioning yourselves directly above one another where possible, and recognize that exposed terrain or active rockfall may need a different way forward.

Ascending on scree can be, as McEleney puts it, a little “soul-destroying.” As tempting as it might be to rush through it, picking up the pace rarely does you any favors.

It has been revealed that rather than heading straight up a scree field, look for a way to link patches of larger, more stable rock, or take a switchbacking approach where there isn’t an established trail and you can avoid damaging vegetation. Martin also looks for well-traveled tracks through smaller rocks, where previous foot traffic might have compressed some of the loose material. If there’s an established trail through the scree, stick to it.

In softer scree, McEleney sometimes kicks steps into the slope, either to uncover more stable ground beneath the loose rock or to give his hiking partners a series of footsteps to follow.

Recent findings suggest that and before resigning yourself to a particularly miserable slog, take another look around. Is there a way to skirt the scree field altogether, or to intercept it higher up the mountainside? Sometimes the easiest way up a scree field is to spend as little time on it as possible. Sometimes, it’s better to slide down and around.

Unlike plunge stepping, where you’re trying to dig your heel into the mountainside with each step, scree surfing (sometimes called scree skiing) involves intentionally sliding with the loose rock beneath your feet.

“The whole slope wants to go downhill anyway,” McEleney indicates. “You can just sort of ride it.”.

Industry observers note that on a slope of fine scree with a safe runout and nobody below you, start by taking a few deliberate downhill steps. You may find that the rock continues to move beneath your foot after you’ve planted it. Get comfortable with that sensation before attempting to intentionally slide. McEleney considers the first 50 to 100 feet an “information gathering phase,” during which he gets a feel for how much the material moves beneath him.

When surfing, McEleney likens his stance to that of a telemark skier. He keeps his feet about shoulder-width apart, one slightly ahead of the other, in what he describes as an “athletic stance,” allowing him to react as the rock shifts beneath him.

On particularly fine, deep scree, McEleney sometimes takes little bounding steps. Rather than trying to find a stationary foothold with each step, you’re allowing the mountain to carry you a little farther downhill. Keep your trekking poles handy for balance, prioritize control over speed, and pay particular attention to any changes in the size or depth of the rock ahead of you.

Not all scree is surfable, though, and not all guides are particularly fond of the technique.

“I’m not afraid of a standing glissade on snow, but I’m pretty worried about scree skiing,” Martin says. “I never feel like I have that much control.”.

According to recent reports, martin feels more in control on softer, lower-angle slopes. A thin layer of gravel over hard ground, for instance, is considerably less forgiving than a deep bed of loose rock.

In a recent development, if you’re shouldering a particularly major pack or nearing the end of a long day, McEleney recommends taking a more conservative approach. If the terrain is unforgiving, your legs are shot, or you’re unsure of your ability to control a slide, there’s no shame in picking your way down the mountainside.

According to recent reports, but if you do decide to send it, it’s a blast. For once, those little rocks that robbed you of your hard-earned elevation on the way up are working in your favor. Enjoy it: You can empty your shoes at the trailhead.
