    46 Gifts For Tweens & Teens That Won't Get An Eye-Roll (Probably)

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4153 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

    ⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Here are the gifts that’ll actually pass the vibe check.
    • Buying gifts for tweens and teens can be a special kind of holiday torture.
    • Industry observers note that since many of us on the Scary Mommy team are living with these outspoken arbiters of taste, we’ve done the reconnaissance for you.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Here are the gifts that’ll actually pass the vibe check.

    Buying gifts for tweens and teens can be a special kind of holiday torture. Don’t get us wrong; it’s so much fun when you get it right. But it doesn’t always go that way, largely because their likes and wants are a moving target. Last year they wanted everything from the toy aisle. Now they want... a hoodie? A lip balm that ~everyone~ has? “Just money”? And boy, if you get it wrong, they’ll let you know. (It’s in the eyes.).

    Industry observers note that since many of us on the Scary Mommy team are living with these outspoken arbiters of taste, we’ve done the reconnaissance for you. Some of these gifts are cozy staples they’ll wear on repeat until spring, like ultra-soft sweats. Some are creative outlets that aren’t too “kiddish,” like a retro digital camera. And some are the niche little things they’ll be weirdly thrilled to find in their stocking, like cloud-shaped body mists.

    Basically, it’s a substantial ol’ list of things they’ll love... even if they’d never admit it out loud.

    Industry observers note that this is exactly the kind of open-ended, screen-free creative experience that I actually feel good putting under the tree. The Charmspring Create Kit Enchanted is developed by childhood experts and designed to spark genuine imagination and independent play, which means I hand it over to my daughter and she disappears into her own world for a very satisfying amount of time. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

    I got these for my athlete nephew, who had previously informed me that Bruce Bolt is THE BEST brand, full stop. I’ll admit I checked them out when they arrived, and I was seriously impressed by the quality. They feel incredible, look super cool (this electric-pink-aqua-blue combo was my nephew’s top pick), and the super-grippy palm is designed for confident catches. He’s worn these — along with the tackified compression arm sleeves — to his games this season, and swears they’re magic. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

    It has been revealed that these cloud-shaped body mists are cute enough to be a bag charm (trending) but durable enough to stand up to the wear and tear of living on a middle schooler's backpack. The scents are just right for the tween and teen age group too — not too childish, but not too mature either. I gave two of them to my 13-year-old niece, who used them up, and I love them as a stocking stuffer idea! — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

    Recent findings suggest that in the summer, the teens wear their Birkenstocks, and in the winter they switch to their UGGs — it is just the way of the world. I have declared these shoes too expensive to purchase as regular school clothes, so my daughter has appealed to Santa for help. He obliges. And since my kids also refuse to wear coats all winter, I'm happy to at least get them in some shoes that have a fuzzy lining. And for purchasing, I can't say it enough: Always go through Zappos so you can exchange and return things while dealing with the best customer service ever. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social.

    The Huffy GRM is exactly the kind of big holiday gift that makes a kid absolutely lose it on Christmas morning! The 24-inch frame is perfect for older kids ready to upgrade from their first bike, and the GRM has a sleek, sporty look that feels genuinely cool rather than obviously like a kids’ bike. It comes mostly assembled right out of the box so the Christmas morning setup is not a three-hour ordeal, and Huffy has been making reliable, fun bikes for decades at a price point that makes a big gift actually achievable. — Katie Garrity.

    My 15-year-old and I are both big Grace & Stella fans, so we were pumped to try these upcoming Luscious Lip Gloss Butters. They did not disappoint! They glide on smooth and dewy, not sticky, and they smell amazing too. My favorite detail is the little keychain attachment, so my daughter can clip it to her backpack or keys and always have it on hand (read: stop “borrowing” mine). These would make a great stocking stuffer for any tween or teen. — Julie Sprankles.

    Sources indicate that seriously, how cute is this? My tween with long, straight hair is ready for her own arsenal of haircare products, and I desperately need her to stop stealing stuff from my bathroom, including my hair dryer. I love how fun this is, I love the accessories, and I love how it's affordable but from a really trusted haircare brand. We went with the pink. — Sarah Aswell.

    Recent findings suggest that for the tween or teen on your list who could use a little support in the self-care and mental wellness department, a Therabox subscription is one of the most thoughtful gifts you can give. Each monthly box is curated by licensed therapists and packed with full-size wellness and self-care products designed to support emotional health, reduce stress, and encourage healthy habits. It arrives like a gift every single month, which makes it the present that keeps going long after the holidays are over, and the therapist-curated angle means every product inside actually has a purpose beyond just smelling nice. It’s a gift that indicates “I see you and I want you to feel good” in the most tangible way possible! — Katie Garrity.

    I have two tweens who are total musicheads, so I knew they’d flip for this Marshall Emberton III portable speaker. It’s a total upgrade from tinny phone audio, with that classic, cool Marshall look and full 360-degree sound. As a mom, I really appreciate that it’s built to handle real life: dustproof, waterproof, and the battery lasts 32+ hours on a single charge. — Julie Sprankles.

    Sources indicate that practically every child I know is into some form of lip balm, which is great because personally I didn't discover it until much later in life and now adore it, too. These lip balms make a great stocking stuffer: they're cute, they smell awesome (they come in kid-friendly flavors like "Frosted Sugar Plum" and "Candy Cane Fluff), and they're affordable. Add to cart stat. — Kate Auletta.

    Sources indicate that sometimes my teen's Christmas list just looks like a list of hoodies. One of her all-time favorites is this fresh classic from Hollister. These are super soft and oversized (but not huge), making it easily fall into the "my favorite hoodie" territory. I also bought these for my boy nephews for the holidays — you just really can't go wrong with these, I swear. — Sarah Aswell.

    It has been revealed that this sleep set has completely changed our bedtime routine. The Dreamjellie pillow is designed specifically for kids and teens, with a shape that supports proper alignment whether they sleep on their side, back, or stomach, and the whole set comes with everything needed for a genuinely cozy, sleep-optimized setup. Getting a tween to actually wind down and sleep well is one of the great challenges of this age, and having bedding that feels special and is actually designed for their bodies makes a real difference. — Katie Garrity.

    This might be the gift that gets the biggest reaction from my gamer teen this year! It snaps right onto their phone and turns it into a handheld gaming console, with full-size joysticks and rear buttons, plus a comfy ergonomic grip. It works with almost any game that supports controllers, from Roblox and Minecraft to Xbox and PlayStation remote play. They can even go wireless and play on a tablet, PC, or TV! My husband fully looks forward to helping my son “test” this out when it comes in. — Julie Sprankles.

    Industry observers note that I have a feeling many tween girls in my life will live for this gift: It’s a locket and strawberry-scented lipgloss in one. The lip gloss is cruelty-free, nut-free, and gluten-free, and is gentle enough for little kids to use over and over again. I also love that, once the gloss is gone, a message reading “You Are Super!” appears. I couldn’t love this more. — Kate Auletta.

    Industry observers note that this is a newly introduced brand for me, but they have so many cute, affordable clothes that really seem to speak to my two teen kids. This double-layered shirt creates such a cool look (SO reminiscent of 90s Delia's, by the way), and it doesn't break the bank. I feel like I can buy a few cute shirts from here and make my kid's whole month. — Sarah Aswell.

    According to recent reports, for the tween or teen who is living on their phone camera but deserves something that actually feels like a real creative tool, the Lola is the answer. The silver color is genuinely stunning and the kind of thing a style-conscious tween will want to carry everywhere and photograph everything with. — Katie Garrity.

    According to recent reports, both of my teens love to create fun little skits and videos as a creative outlet, so I figured it was time to get them an actual tripod instead of watching them precariously balance their phones on random objects to get the shot. I like that this one extends up to 71 inches, and that the Bluetooth works from up to 33 feet away. Plus, it folds down to 13 inches and weighs about a pound, making it easy to toss in a backpack. Oh, and it’s super affordable! — Julie Sprankles.

    I’m sort of like a tween in that I, too, live for a ridiculously fun bag. What I love about this is that you can position the bear (it also comes as a panda, unicorn, and fuzzy heart) to look like it's hugging you. It’s completely adorable and makes a great gift for tweens everywhere. — Kate Auletta.

    It has been revealed that my 11-year-old is an art fanatic, but finding the right kits for her can be hard, as a lot of stuff is a little too "kidish." But she loves these eraser kits by Pretty Pixel, which allow her to either use templates or create her own characters. She loves making erasers for friends or challenging herself to make her favorite anime characters. One thing I love? The kits to buy more eraser materials are super affordable. — Sarah Aswell.

    Industry observers note that for the Swiftie on your list who has everything, this is the gift that genuinely surprises them. Historic Newspapers compiles real newspaper coverage of Taylor Swift’s career from her earliest days all the way through her record-breaking eras, printed and bound into a beautiful keepsake book that reads like a time capsule of pop culture history. It is the kind of deeply personal, one-of-a-kind gift that no amount of merch shopping replicates, and for a tween or teen who has grown up watching Taylor dominate the world, seeing it all documented in real news print is going to hit differently. — Katie Garrity.

    Industry observers note that if your teen’s bedroom doubles as a gaming den (hi, my son), let me put you on these Nanoleaf Blocks! They combine customizable smart lighting with shelves and pegboards so your gamer can mix and build a custom wall feature around their PC. They also connect with other Nanoleaf products, so the system can grow with them. But the reactive lighting is the real showstopper: When my son plays a game, the blocks’ lighting shifts to match the colors on his screen, creating a super-cool immersive experience. — Julie Sprankles.

    I'm a fan of anything that gets my kids off screens, and this Camp Snap Mini Camcorder did not come to play. It's compact, it's screen-free, and it has point-and-shoot recording (just like the old days!) with five film-inspired filters. There's no playback screen, no Wi-Fi, and no apps required — what a welcome change, huh? Definitely getting this for my older kid for Christmas. — Kate Auletta.

    Recent findings suggest that this brand, SMOKO, has so many cute things that both of my teens would gladly die for. But this couch potato drinking a boba tea? That lets you turn off the overhead lights that my children hate with their whole hearts? Priceless. These are at a great price point, too, for things like friends' birthday gifts. — Sarah Aswell.

    Industry observers note that cloud Nine’s sweatpants have a reputation that genuinely precedes them. The fabric is that buttery, weightless softness kids refuse to take off once they put them on, and for a tween with strong opinions about comfort, this is basically a guaranteed win. They are the kind of cozy, elevated loungewear that looks cute enough to wear out but feels good enough to sleep in, which at this age is basically the holy grail of getting dressed. — Katie Garrity.

    According to recent reports, these I Love Aromie Bakery plushies are adorable and smell SO good. Snuggymug is a cuddly little hot cocoa puppy, and when you squeeze his ear, his cheeks light up and he releases a visible puff of chocolate-scented mist. (Yes, really... it’s magical.) It’s a super-fun sensory gift that’s equal parts cuddle buddy and collectible. There are six characters, and I have no doubt my teens will not rest until they have all of them! — Julie Sprankles.

    Industry observers note that my kids are sadly growing out of the matching family pajama era — it's just too babyish for them. But luckily for me, there are some more teen-friendly options out there that work for everyone. I LOVE these Sunshine Society silky jammies that feel amazing and also have a really fun print that even the most eye-rolling teen will accept into their lives. — Sarah Aswell.

    If your tween goes through hair ties like they’re disappearing into a black hole, this set is a lifesaver because it comes with 36 clips, bands, and barrettes in a bright mix of colors. It all lives in its own organizer case, which means her accessories finally have a home that isn’t the bottom of a backpack or your car’s cup holder. At $12, it’s the kind of stocking stuffer or small gift she’ll actually use every single day! — Katie Garrity.

    I got these CMF Clip Pro earbuds for my teen, who immediately fell in love with the coral colorway. (It’s so pretty!) They have an open-ear clip design, so instead of jamming buds into her ears, they hug the outside of the ear. This makes them (a) stay put and (b) actually comfortable to wear. The sound is really fantastic, too, with hi-res audio and clear voice technology for calls. — Julie Sprankles.

    My daughter informs me that these hoodies are THE COOLEST. Hoodies that can be layered and hoodies with buttons instead of ties are in, and this has both. And, more importantly to me, Athleta has really nice quality clothes that are nowhere near as expensive as some of the other athleisure brands my daughter yearns for. I got this one on sale for under $30! — Sarah Aswell.

    Buying this for my daughter because it combines two things she’s obsessed with, Squishmallows and anything that’s satisfying to squeeze, into one tiny, glittery package. It’s filled with slow-flow glitter and has a shape-memory design, so no matter how hard she stretches and squishes it, it bounces right back into its Squishmallows shape. At under $10, it’s a great stocking stuffer for any tween who needs something to do with her hands (and honestly, a few moms I know too)! — Katie Garrity.

    Recent findings suggest that these M2U NYC Makeup Blending Sponges are the cutest, most affordable stocking stuffers for tweens or teens who are into makeup. The collection includes four latex-free sponges, each with an adorable animal on its packaging: a rabbit, a panda, a fox, and a cat. Each “animal” does a different job, from precise contouring to blending around tricky spots like the nose and under-eyes. And at only $22 for all four, how could you not? — Julie Sprankles.

    According to recent reports, the problem with tweens is that they say they don't want any toys for Christmas, but when the holiday rolls around and they only get clothes and skincare products, they realize they are sad (and that they are still children who want toys!) For my 11-year-old, the answer was this mini pottery wheel and spin art set. It is fun enough to feel like a toy, but it lets them create cool art and feels kind of just like art supplies. This is also a great birthday present for elementary-aged kids. — Sarah Aswell.

    Recent findings suggest that for the parent who isn’t ready to hand over a smartphone but wants their kid to be reachable, the TickTalk 6 is the middle ground, because it does calls, video calls, real texts, and GPS with zero games, social media, or open internet. You decide who’s on the approved contact list from the app, your kid still gets SOS and 911 calling plus a walkie-talkie feature, and there’s nothing on the watch for her to get sucked into. It’s a big gift, but it’s the one that gives a tween a little independence while you keep the controls. — Katie Garrity.

    Recent findings suggest that I recently discovered Fun Fact Co., and I’m obsessed with how the brand turns educational material into actual art. I have two teens with very different feelings about math: one loves numbers, and the other really struggles with them. This Multiplication Table Print appeals to both of them. It highlights prime, Fibonacci, and square numbers, which gives my math lover something extra to geek out over, while my other kid gets a handy, judgment-free reference tool. And it looks great on our study wall! — Julie Sprankles.

    All my tween daughters want for Christmas is sweatpants. And all I want for Christmas is to find some high-quality, AFFORDABLE sweatpants for my tweens. This pair from Pacsun fits the bill. They're only $35, they come in a rainbow of colors, and the style is really cute. They are "one size fits most," which was a little concerning, but I did find that they fit both my very petite 11-year-old and my athletic almost-14-year-old. So! — Sarah Aswell.

    Sources indicate that for the tween or teen who treats her AirPods like a fashion accessory, a Burga case is the cool-girl upgrade that makes the boring white case look like part of her outfit. It comes in a ton of printed designs, gives the case 360° protection from drops and scratches, still works with wireless charging, and even lets the LED light show through. It also clips right onto a backpack or belt loop with the included carabiner, which means it’s a whole lot harder to lose and a whole lot more stylish to carry! — Katie Garrity.

    Sources indicate that for years, I always forgot to get my kids presents they could use in the summer — but I'm not making that mistake anymore. I always get my kids a swimsuit and cover-up, and I always get them a game that's fun to play outside. This year, I got them Basa, which is a four-person paddle game that's easy to set up anywhere you have enough open space, from the grass to sand. I love that this has the feel of pickleball but you don't need to seek out a court, and that it's easy to start playing right away. — Sarah Aswell.

    I will admit this gift may be more for me than my teen, but still... I stand by the fact that it makes a great gift if, like me, you have a upcoming driver in the house. This little treasure plugs right into their car’s diagnostic port and connects to a phone over Bluetooth, so if that dreaded “check engine” light pops on, my teen can see what’s wrong right away, along with verified repair suggestions. It’s a smart way to teach a new driver some basic car care, and I appreciate that it’s a one-time purchase with no subscription required. — Julie Sprankles.

    Recent findings suggest that I don't want my kid to grow up without experiencing music the way I did: listening to entire albums, offline. And the cool part is that kids are discovering their parents' CD collections just like we discovered our parents' record collections. For under $100, Lola has released a rechargeable, portable CD player that comes with wired headphones included. The only real differences? This has a great anti-skip feature, and it can be charged via a USB port. Um, I kind of want one too? — Sarah Aswell.

    Industry observers note that for the tween or teen who needs a break from holiday chaos, this winter-themed bath bomb is a little spa moment she can fizz away in, with a light blue and white design covered in an icy snowflake pattern. It melts into glistening blue water scented with eucalyptus, peppermint, and lemongrass oils for a cool, fresh, tingly bath that feels like a snow day without the cold. It’s made in Canada, arrives with no packaging, and it’s a perfect, easy stocking stuffer for any bath-loving kid on your list! — Katie Garrity.

    It has been revealed that my artsy teen would take one of these coloring blankets in every single design if they could, and would happily gift one to each of their friends too. Each 50-by-60-inch blanket comes printed with an original design by a Minnesota-based artist, from galaxies to vintage florals, ready to color in. We have the under-the-sea version, and we’ve been totally nerding out over all the cool sea creatures to fill in. It’s such a fun, creative, cozy outlet that turns into a one-of-a-kind keepsake. Bonus: It’s from a woman-owned business! — Julie Sprankles.

    Recent findings suggest that for the teen who’s into Pilates, barre, yoga, or just wants the cutest cozy socks, these grippy full-foot socks are a $16 stocking stuffer she’ll actually wear, in a pretty green with a little yellow “namaste” on them. They have a no-slip grip on the bottom, a cushioned terry footbed, compression arch support, and a padded ankle rest, all in soft, moisture-wicking cotton. They’re snug and supportive without feeling stiff, which makes them the perfect gift for the kid who is always stretching, sliding around the house, or heading to class. — Katie Garrity.

    Recent findings suggest that this is my artsy daughter's BIG holiday present, and she is absolutely going to flip out. I have gotten her so many markers over the years, and these are her absolute favorites to work with. And as she's graduated from Crayola to more grown-up art needs, this organization has been really great for us. I also love that this comes in a sturdy carrying case and with a swatch card, which my daughter loves to fill out as soon as she gets a fresh set. — Sarah Aswell.

    In a recent development, for the tween or teen who's obsessed with her dog (or everyone else's), this dog-themed earring set from Pip Pop Post is a super cute way to show it off. The earrings are made from hypoallergenic 18k gold-plated stainless steel with colorful enamel, and they're free of nickel, lead, and copper, so they're comfortable for sensitive ears. They use flat screw-back posts that stay put through sleep, sports, and school, and they're waterproof and sweat-proof, so she can wear them 24/7 without a second thought! — Katie Garrity.

    Every year, we get the kids a holiday-themed puzzle from Mudpuppy. The quality is great, and the puzzles are challenging without being a nightmare. Many of them have foil details, which make them so pretty and fun. Especially as my kids get older and there are fewer traditional toys under the tree, having a puzzle to settle around on Christmas afternoon while we watch 'Miracle on 34th Street 'is a real crowd-pleaser. — Sarah Aswell.

    If you were a kid in the ‘90s like I was, you probably remember the absolute thrill of a fresh pack of Gelly Roll pens. Well, I’m happy to report they’re still just as magical for tweens and teens today! This 74-pen gift set from Sakura has every color imaginable, from metallics to bright neons, and I know my artsy teen is going to flip when they find it under the tree. The pens are perfect for doodling, coloring, junk journaling, or even just making handmade cards for friends (one of my teen’s favorite hobbies). And, yes, I’ll obviously be borrowing a few for my own desk. — Julie Sprankles.

    #55977. 10 Great Sports Docs & True-Life Stories To Stream With Your Kids Right Now

    📅 15 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1158 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

    10 Great Sports Docs & True-Life Stories To Stream With Your Kids Right Now

    📅 15 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1158 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • From inspiring stories to crucial moments in history to cutting edge contermporary atheletes, there’s a great co-viewing experience for everyone.
    • Recent findings suggest that finding movies and TV that please everyone can be tough.
    • Sports docuseries, or true-to-life dramatized sports stories, are great to watch with young athletes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From inspiring stories to crucial moments in history to cutting edge contermporary atheletes, there’s a great co-viewing experience for everyone.

    Recent findings suggest that finding movies and TV that please everyone can be tough. But if you’ve got a sporty kid, screen time is a great opportunity. Sure, there’s old-school sports movie like The Sandlot or A League of Their Own — complete with inspirational messages and strong moral codes. But why go for fictional sports stories when you can get the real thing?

    Sports docuseries, or true-to-life dramatized sports stories, are great to watch with young athletes. They tell inspirational tales and maybe even give them a real-life role model in the meantime. From a variety of different sports to a selection of different formats, we’ve thought about the watchability and the relevance of each of these selections. There should be something for everyone in this list. And, at the very least, with each, you and your kid will learn something.

    This documentary film focuses on several different Paralympic athletes, all of whom have truly amazing stories. Warning for parents: This documentary is not for the faint of heart, as some of the physical challenges are truly harrowing. For example, Bebe Vio — who inspired the name of the documentary — lost all of her limbs to meningitis at the age of 11. She nonetheless went on to become a wheelchair fencer. Deeply inspiring, this doc is great for teens interested in sports and perhaps great for all of us to have a little perspective on the amazing nature of the human spirit.

    In a recent development, the 2004 story of the Boston Red Sox is a great one in terms of an underdog story. Even if you’re not a Red Sox fan, this story represents a very specific time in baseball and tells the story of how this iconic team broke a curse that had existed since 1918. If your kid is just starting to get into baseball, this documentary series might seem like ancient history; after all, 2004 was more than 20 years ago. And yet, this particular season for many of us feels very recent and still relevant.

    Who doesn’t love trick shots? This 30 for 30 ESPN doc is all about a group of five guys who were former college roommates who created a sports comedy entertainment phenomenon. Focused on trick shots and betting, this doc is 100% for older kids. But if you’ve got a teen who is into sports and loves to joke around, this is a great, quirky documentary focused on male friendship, humor, and creating something nobody has ever done before.

    In a recent development, everybody is obsessed with Travis Kelce, but his brother Jason Kelce might be the more interesting of the siblings, at least as an athlete. The 2023 documentary film chronicles the 2022 Philadelphia Eagles season, with a specific focus on Kelce. The main tension here is whether or not Kelce will retire from the NFL. Weird topic for kids? Well, for tweens and teens interested in unpacking the real-deal toll of being in the NFL, there’s something smartly educational about this. You may be young and obsessed with football now, but life is long.

    Not technically a documentary, this is a docudrama based on the true story of Ray McElrathbey, who deals with a ton of family adversity and racism. Set in the early 2000s, McElrathbey’s story is inspiring and very family-oriented. Again, this one might be for older kids, but the script is from Nick Santora of Reacher and Sopranos fame, so there’s a breezy and very focused feeling to this movie.

    It has been revealed that here’s another docudrama that is based on a real-life movement in India, centered on teenagers and skateboarding culture. In the film, a young girl named Prerna (Rachel Sanchita Gupta) finds purpose and belonging through skateboarding. The film is a heartwarming coming-of-age movie, but watching it with your kid means you’re also giving them a dose of contemporary history. The production for the film also worked very closely with rural villages in India to make sure it accurately portrayed the culture and struggles of teenagers.

    A great one to watch with your aspiring skateboarding kid, or maybe a kid who isn’t sure what their athletic interest might be.

    One of the greatest athletes of our time is also the subject of a one-of-a-kind docuseries. Released in 2024, Simone Biles Rising is all about the gymnast’s comeback. The fact that Biles has been so transparent about her mental health has been a groundbreaking part of the conversations about young athletes. As both a role model and someone who is part of living history, Biles is a figure that should inspire conversation with your curious athlete.

    This 10-part documentary changed everything back in 2020. However, at this point, The Last Dance — which tells the story of one of the greatest periods of the Chicago Bulls — almost feels vintage. Chances are, for certain parents, you didn’t have a kid old enough to watch this documentary nearly seven years ago. And, if you’re of the generation that lived through the Bulls’ 1990s dynasty, then you owe it to share that history with your kid.

    Not everything about Michael Jordan and his teammates is admirable, to be clear. But the thing about some great sports history is that it can be messy.

    It has been revealed that focused on the 2024 X Games, The Rise: Gold Medal Girls of the X Games focuses on four teen athletes, Arisa Trew, Shiloh Catori, Reese Nelson, and Jada Ward. Those are all skateboarders, and that’s just the most recent season. More broadly, The Rise covers all sorts of women’s sports, from skating to the WNBA. If you have a young woman looking for some fresh role models, you can’t miss with the various seasons of The Rise.

    You can really start anywhere with this excellent docuseries. But the most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained is focused on the 2024 Tour de France. Obviously, the famous bicycle race has existed since 1903, but it’s really only recently that we could actually document this incredible event. Even the least sporty kid in the world can get excited about people using their bodies to propel a bicycle forward. And the most sporty kids will have trouble wrapping their mind around the sheer effort it takes to traverse 2,200 miles over 24 days over some of the hilliest terrain on Earth.

    The most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained, released in 2025, is now the last season of this docuseries. The real Tour de France hasn’t gone anywhere, of course. In fact, it’s happening right now. Meaning if you get your kid excited enough, you can watch the 2026 Tour de France as it’s happening. Or watch a little contemporary Tour de France, then go back and watch Unchained on Netflix.

    #55976. I'm Not A "Bowel Normie" & I Still Have Three Healthy Kids

    📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1011 w)

    I'm Not A "Bowel Normie" & I Still Have Three Healthy Kids

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1011 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life.
    • Sources indicate that I became sick when I was 12.
    • In a recent development, over the next three years, I spent much of my time in doctor’s offices and bathrooms, with bloating, constipation, diarrhea and bleeding.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life.

    Sources indicate that I became sick when I was 12. It happened out of nowhere. We were on a family trip to Fresh York City to celebrate New Year’s Eve in Times Square. I stood out on the Statue of Liberty’s crown, sipping the (extravagantly priced) hot chocolate my parents bought me to combat the cold, gazing in awe at the dazzling metropolis, and was suddenly overcome with nausea. That night, I began vomiting, running to the toilet, and developed a high fever. I couldn’t even make it to the window to see the ball drop.

    In a recent development, over the next three years, I spent much of my time in doctor’s offices and bathrooms, with bloating, constipation, diarrhea and bleeding. I was in pain, mostly searing pangs. Who knew when they would hit? I went for X-rays, scopes, breath tests, physical exams; I tried medications, carbon supplements, acupuncture. Steroids worked miraculously at first, then not at all. Experimental drugs went through me completely undigested. I began to evacuate the lining of my own colon; it looked like a thin white snake. My blood count was so low I was repeatedly hospitalized for blood transfusions and iron infusions. It appeared I had very severe ulcerative colitis.

    During this time, I was in 7th to 10th grades, the time of first loves, frenemies, tattoos and drivers ed. But as someone with acute bowel disease, my teenage life was increasingly limited. Want a ride home? No thanks. I was worried that whoever was driving would take detours, keeping me away from a toilet. The metro was scary; what if it stalled and I was stuck? I went to school but sat next to the door of the classroom. It was hard for me to go to boy-girl get-togethers: I couldn’t even sit through a movie in someone’s basement, and what if the bathroom was within earshot? The logistics were so difficult, the risk of embarrassment too high. I stopped attending most things.

    It has been revealed that all teenagers deal with their body changing, with it being out of their control. My body was waging war on me, emitting shameful sounds, smells and sights without my consent. It felt like I, Little Judy, was buried somewhere deep inside this morass of sickly flesh, this thing that all these ancient doctors were probing, trying to decipher. Had I done something to cause this? Was it my fault? I didn’t not-love my body, I hated it.

    According to recent reports, when my friends were exploring sexuality, I recoiled. For one, it’s hard to think about smooching when you’re doubled down in anguish. Constantly exposed to the medical world, I’d created strong barriers, dissociating from my physical experience.

    Not to mention, how could I possibly share what I was going through with anyone? My peers were worried about algebra tests; I was worried about blood tests. My friends gossiped about trying drugs; I was on more drugs than half the school combined! I went to doctors who mentioned the possibility of developing cancer. I felt misunderstood, alone, and so very ugly. I didn’t know how to let anyone get close.

    By tenth grade, my life was completely in the toilet, literally. Surgery was offered as an option. Major surgery: they would remove my entire large intestine colon and create a pouch from part of the small intestine that would, hopefully, work as a de facto colon. Doctors kept postponing the procedure, worried about the risks. But I insisted on the operation. I told my parents, if they didn’t take me, I’d take the bus.

    So, at 15, I had my entire colon removed. My pouch was amazing; I was not a “bowel normie,” and I couldn’t eat with abandon, but I lived a mostly pain-free life. I remained relatively healthy through my twenties, eventually dating (and making up for lost time!). I got married at age 31 to a man who I was able to open up to about my chronic condition, and who was willing to support my toilet paper habit. But then came the question: was my body robust enough to have a baby? Could I get past all my shame, all my corporeal disappointment, to create a life? And should I be a parent, i.e. would my children end up sick too? I wobbled for two years.

    Sources indicate that then, the second I’d decided to maybe even consider trying to get pregnant, my gynecologist enrolled me in a fertility clinic, saying, “People with your surgeries have so much trouble, there’s not a minute to waste.” A few weeks later, I was doing bloodwork at my local clinic so they could send the results to the fertility center. Only, it turned out, as a squealing nurse revealed, I was already pregnant.

    Sources indicate that the nine months passed seamlessly, bowel-wise, except for some excruciating bouts of gas that had become trapped under my growing belly. My first daughter was born healthy via C-section (recommended, as natural childbirth carried a risk of damaging the pouch). Though I did have a dangerous and frightening ectopic pregnancy a few years later when trying for my second — most likely due to scar tissue from the old surgery — I ultimately ended up having three children which is a miracle, and also, a little insane. My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life! Never mind years of yoga and pilates, finally, I felt strong. And even, a little bit beautiful.

    Judy Batalion is a New York Times bestselling author of award-winning nonfiction and fiction. Her essays have appeared in The New York Times, The Washington Post, and Vogue, among others. Judy has a BA in the History of Science from Harvard, a PhD from the University of London, and has worked as a museum curator and university lecturer. She lives in New York City with her husband and three children.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that each November, Google gives us a peek behind the curtain, synthesising billions of shopping-related searches into their Holiday 100 Gift Guide.
    • Here are the trending toys parents will want to know about, plus what the list claims about how we’re shopping this year.
    • Searches for “classic toy train set” climbed 240% this year, one of the biggest jumps Google shared.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that each November, Google gives us a peek behind the curtain, synthesising billions of shopping-related searches into their Holiday 100 Gift Guide. The list is built from a full year of Search trends across every category from tech to style. And this year, the toys and games section looks suspiciously like the inside of an elder millennial’s childhood toy chest.

    Here are the trending toys parents will want to know about, plus what the list claims about how we’re shopping this year.

    Searches for “classic toy train set” climbed 240% this year, one of the biggest jumps Google shared. Wooden trains survive toddler teeth, being thrown down the stairs and never fail to get passed down more than once. (Expect the figure-eight to claim your living room floor for the next few years.).

    “A ton of play,” Google wrote, and we respect the pun. Searches for stuffed elephant plushies rose 240%, with the Pets Alive Baby Elephant Surprise as the featured pick. Plush is a good pick for a 1-year-old and a 10-year-old alike, and the right one becomes a friend for life.

    Searches for the Fujifilm instax holiday set jumped 190%. For tweens, a camera that spits out a real photo is a nice break from the phone, and the prints end up taped to bedroom walls instead of buried in a camera roll. They’ll fly through the film, so tuck a couple of extra packs in the box.

    Industry observers note that searches for the FAO Schwarz Piano Mat “struck a chord,” rising 180% in 2026. Anyone who watched Tom Hanks stomp out a duet on the giant keyboard in “Major” wanted one of these, and the floor-sized version now fits in a playroom. It’s a sneaky music-and-movement toy for preschoolers. It’s also loud, so choose its permanent residence carefully.

    In a recent development, searches for “adjustable roller skates” cruised up 180%. Adjustable skates expand across several sizes, so they can outlast a growth spurt or two. Just remember to add a helmet and pads to the cart.

    Some of this may come down to who’s doing the shopping. Millennials make up a big share of today’s parents, and plenty of us spent our childhoods at the roller rink, building wooden train tracks across the living room rug and waiting for Polaroids to develop. (By impatiently wagging them back and forth, of course.) It’s not hard to imagine a few of these searches coming from parents trying to hand down something that felt magic to them. The best part? There’s a good chance they’ll all still be in rotation when next year’s list comes out.

    #55972. Get Into a Back-to-School Mindset With Advice From 12 Youth Soccer Coaches

    📅 16 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2125 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

    Get Into a Back-to-School Mindset With Advice From 12 Youth Soccer Coaches

    📅 16 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2125 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Start the school year off on the right foot with insights from coaches who understand how the game translates to life off the field.
    • According to recent reports, late summer is always the hardest on parents.
    • The back-to-school transition is never the clean handoff the calendar makes it look like.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Start the school year off on the right foot with insights from coaches who understand how the game translates to life off the field.

    According to recent reports, late summer is always the hardest on parents. The pool days are numbered. The long evenings are shortening. The school year is coming, and it doesn’t care how ready you are.

    The back-to-school transition is never the clean handoff the calendar makes it look like. Every August, we tell ourselves this year will be different. You’ll get ahead of it. Lunch prep sorted by Sunday. Bedtime routine locked in a week early. Screen-time rules clearly communicated and actually enforced. You’ll draw up this plan with the kind of granular, paranoid attention to detail that Guardiola brings to a cup final. But then, it’s all a disaster by Tuesday.

    If you’re looking for an actual strategy that holds up, go to the park on a Saturday morning, find the sideline, and start listening to whoever is coaching.

    In a recent development, these are people managing every extreme of human emotion — low blood sugar, wounded pride, full-on existential crises — all while trying to stop a five-way argument over who gets the neon green goalie pinnies. If they don’t know something useful, nobody does. So we hit up a dozen youth soccer coaches for their best back-to-school advice.

    I tell my girls this on the first day of every season, and I mean it every time. Some days we’re doing your favorite thing. Some days we’re doing the thing you hate. The thing you hate is usually the thing that needs work. That’s not a coincidence. I don’t let them skip the hard drills because they don’t feel like it. I don’t let them drift to the stuff they’re already good at and call it practice. That’s not practice. That’s just playing around.

    The subject your kid is dreading going back to — that’s the one. That’s the drill they need to run. Don’t negotiate them out of it. Make the deal: Do the work first, then we talk. It’s the same conversation I have at practice every Tuesday and Thursday, and it works there, too.

    I don’t do massive speeches. I never have. I’ve seen coaches do the whole thing — the whiteboard, the clipboard, the fire-and-brimstone season opener — and the kids are bored by the second sentence. So I just ask one question: What kind of teammate do you want? And they tell me. Funny. Helpful. Somebody who doesn’t make you feel bad when you mess up. Somebody who actually passes the ball. I write it all down. Then I say, good — now be all of that.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s not complicated. It’s just that nobody asks them the question directly and then holds them to the answer. Try it before school starts. Ask your kid what kind of friend they want to have this year. Then have the second half of that conversation.

    Industry observers note that I’ve been doing this since before most of these parents were driving their kids to practice, and the one thing that has never changed is this: Effort is the one thing every single kid controls completely. Talent, you’re born with, or you’re not. Height, same thing. But running back on defense when you’re tired? Picking yourself up after a bad touch and going again? That’s a choice. I’ve had kids with every physical tool in the world coast through and wonder why they weren’t improving. I’ve had kids who couldn’t trap a ball if their life depended on it go on to be captains because they simply refused to stop working.

    In a recent development, teachers see it the same way I do. The kid who stays after, asks questions, turns things in on time — that kid builds a reputation. And that reputation opens doors that talent alone doesn’t.

    It has been revealed that every season, I get at least one kid who shows up on day one with opinions. Wants to play a different position, run a different shape, do things the way her last team did it. And look — I love that. I want players who think about the game. But there’s an order of operations. You don’t get to redesign a system you don’t understand yet. So the rule is: First month, you learn why we do what we do. Why we press from the front. Why we switch the point of attack the way we do.

    Once you understand the why, then you’ve earned the right to push back.

    Industry observers note that A newly introduced school year means new teachers with their own ways of doing things. The kid who spends the first few weeks actually paying attention — figuring out how this classroom works before deciding what they think of it — that kid is so far ahead of the one who comes in with their arms already crossed.

    It has been revealed that I have a rule on this team, and it has been the same rule since my first season: You get three seconds after a mistake. Three seconds to be upset, to be frustrated, to feel whatever you feel. Then your head comes back up, and you get back in position. Because here’s the thing: The play is still happening. The game didn’t stop because you had a bad touch. And if you’re standing there feeling sorry for yourself, you’re now two mistakes deep instead of one.

    I tell parents this, too, because it applies to everything. Your kid is going to fail a test this year. They’re going to say something wrong in class and feel embarrassed about it. They’re going to have a bad day. In life situations off the field, you get more than three seconds, but the same lesson applies. Acknowledge the mistake and then head up, back in position. The recovery is the name of the game.

    Industry observers note that I am obsessive about communication on the field. Obsessive. Not yelling, not blaming — information. Constant, useful, real-time information between players. Where you are, what you see, what they should do next. Most kids go completely silent under pressure, and that is exactly backwards from what you need. When it’s hardest to talk is when talking matters most.

    I tell my players: A quiet team is a confused team. And a confused team gives the ball away. It’s the same thing off the field. The kid who speaks up in class, who says hi to the kid sitting alone at lunch, who tells a friend when something’s wrong — that kid ends up in the middle of things. The good things. Make some noise this year. Say something.

    Industry observers note that I played college soccer, and I will tell you that the thing nobody taught me until it was almost too late was how to rest. We were all conditioned to think that more was always better — more sprints, more film, more time in the gym. And there’s a point where more just breaks you. The best thing I ever did for my game was learn to take recovery seriously. Sleep. Real sleep. Not optional, not a treat — part of the program.

    It has been revealed that I build rest into my players’ weeks now, and I don’t let them feel guilty about it. The brain works the same way the body does. It consolidates everything it learned while you sleep. So if your kid is heading back to school and you’re letting them stay up until midnight on their phone — that’s not a small thing. That’s undermining everything they did that day. Rest is not laziness. I promise you it’s not.

    Industry observers note that I’ve been watching kids show up to this field for a long time, and I can tell you — the ones who get there early are different. Not because they’re more talented. Because they’ve had time to settle in. They’ve already touched a ball, already talked to a teammate, already figured out where they are and what they’re doing before anything’s officially started. They’re comfortable. The ones sprinting in right at the whistle are always the ones who take the whole first half to find their rhythm.

    So on the first day of school, get there early. Your kid will have the chance to find the right classroom, ask any questions, and breathe a little bit. It’s a small thing that changes the whole morning.

    I coach little kids. Eight-year-olds. So I see a lot of feelings on this field, and I’ve been real clear about my policy since day one: All the feelings are allowed. You can cry. You can tell me you need a minute. You can be upset. None of that is a problem. What you cannot do is walk off this field and decide you’re done. That’s the one thing I won’t accept. And I don’t say it mean — I just say it clearly, and I say it early, so it’s already been said when the moment comes.

    Back to school is hard for a lot of kids, and I think parents sometimes feel like they’re supposed to pretend it isn’t. The anxiety is real. The overwhelm is real. Your kid can feel all of it and still go. That’s actually the lesson — that you’re allowed to struggle and still show up. Those two things can both be true at the same time.

    Industry observers note that I think about the game the way I think about conversation. There are moments when you have to speak — when you see the opening, and you have to take it, because if you wait, it’ll be gone. And there are moments when the best thing you can do is find the person in a better position and give it to them. The hardest thing to coach is the judgment between those two moments. A player who always shoots is a ball hog. A player who always passes is invisible. The great ones — the really great ones — know the difference in real time.

    Industry observers note that that’s an ego conversation as much as it’s a soccer conversation. Knowing when to speak up in class and when to let someone else take the floor. When to lead a group project and when to step back and support. It’s one of the harder things to teach, and one of the more crucial ones. Start having that conversation now, before the year starts.

    I want my players to come to me. That’s the whole thing. I make myself as available as I possibly can because I know from experience that the kids who ask questions are the ones who get better. Not always the most talented kids — just the ones who seek feedback and then actually do something with it. Every season, the gap I notice most isn’t about skill. It’s about which kids advocate for themselves and which ones wait to be noticed.

    Teachers work the same way I do. They want to help — they really do — but they’re managing a roomful of kids, and they can’t chase all of them down. The ones who stay after, send the email, ask what they missed and what they can do better — those are the ones who get more of the good stuff. It’s not about being the favorite. It’s about knowing how to ask for help. That skill will serve your kid for the rest of their life.

    Recent findings suggest that I coach at the level where it starts to get serious. Parents are thinking about high school rosters, kids are thinking about highlight reels, everybody’s tracking individual stats. And I am here to tell you — from where I stand on this sideline — that the players who make the biggest difference are almost never the ones you’d expect.

    Recent findings suggest that I’ve had physically gifted kids who played every game like it was an audition and made everyone around them worse for it. And I’ve had kids who, by every measurable standard, were average, who won us games because they made their teammates better. They covered for people, they communicated, and they did the stuff that doesn’t show up in the box score.

    Sources indicate that we spend so much time on our kids as individuals — their grades, their performance, their future — that we sometimes forget to teach them how to be good at being part of something. That’s a skill too. Maybe the most crucial one. The school year is long and almost entirely a team sport. Remind them.

    #55970. Digital Detox Gift Guide: 27 Analog Gift Ideas For Lo-Fi Fun

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

    Digital Detox Gift Guide: 27 Analog Gift Ideas For Lo-Fi Fun

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2393 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • From paint-by-numbers to screen-free storytelling, these picks make downtime feel intentional and joyful.
    • We started noticing it last year: Everyone seemed to be craving less screen time, less doomscrolling, fewer cheap dopamine hits.
    • After all, there’s just a special, cozy kind of magic in a night with no screens, isn’t there?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From paint-by-numbers to screen-free storytelling, these picks make downtime feel intentional and joyful.

    We started noticing it last year: Everyone seemed to be craving less screen time, less doomscrolling, fewer cheap dopamine hits. And not only has that trend continued in 2026, but it’s gotten even stronger. If anything, we’re all more fried! So analog is having a full-blown moment, which happily makes for some seriously great gifting.

    After all, there’s just a special, cozy kind of magic in a night with no screens, isn’t there? A puzzle spread across the dining room table. A record spinning while parents dance in the kitchen (and their kids feign disgust in the background). Coloring and baking and crafting and playing board games — comfortcore activities that keep hands busy and minds engaged.

    According to recent reports, so this holiday season, give the gift of logging off. From paint-by-numbers to an heirloom-quality chess set, here are our favorite picks for anyone (yourself included) who’s ready to put the phone in a drawer and be fully present for all the holiday merriment.

    It has been revealed that turn off the TV and start a puzzle! And thanks to Completing The Puzzle, you no longer have the excuse, “But I don't know what to do with it when I'm done!” They've figured that all out for you. Completing The Puzzle is the first-ever puzzle rental subscription with high-quality puzzles delivered right to your door. Once you finish, pack it up, send it back, and wait for your latest one to arrive. — Kate Auletta, Editor in Chief.

    It has been revealed that I have noted for about 100 years that I wanted to get into embroidery. Whenever I see something embroidered at an antique mall or thrift store, I am enchanted, but... they are not cheap. Even thrifted! So, why not make my own? Clever Poppy is the perfect way to get an introduction to embroidery if you're a newbie like me. In their kits, they provide step-by-step instructions as well as everything you need to get started. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

    Recent findings suggest that normalize getting your mom a knit or crochet kit! If they like fiber arts, they will love it. Sometimes people gift me a few balls of yarn, which is amazing, but these kits ensure that I have enough to complete a project. I love Lion Brand's selections, and this cardigan is gorgeous and pretty easy to pull off, too! — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social.

    Recent findings suggest that there’s something so deeply satisfying about dropping the needle on a record. You can’t skip songs, you can’t scroll... you actually listen to an album in its purest form. This record player makes that ritual easy, and it looks good doing it with its cool retro-inspired case and little viewing window. It plays both LPs and singles, and it’s compact enough to move wherever you want. I can’t wait to hit the local thrift stores and start building my vinyl collection. (Worth noting: This turntable does also have Bluetooth!) — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor of Lifestyle & Entertainment.

    In a recent development, for all the readers out there, this is one book accessory I never knew I needed! I throw my book into my bag along with all my other crap and typically end up ruining it with crayon marks or crumbs from my kid's latest half-eaten snack. This protective padded sleeve keeps your current reads safe from crushed pages and bent covers (and mystery stains!). — Katie Garrity.

    Sources indicate that coloring girlies, if you're not using Ohuhu markers, we need to talk! This 104-color pack is my go-to when I'm having a cozy coloring night with my daughter. Plus, these markers have a dual-tip marker design — choose the brush tip for sweeping, calligraphic strokes, or the fine tip for details. — Katie Garrity.

    I’ve got nothing against my Notes app. In fact, I use it all the time. But I will always, always be a girlie who loves a really beautiful notebook and the way it makes me want to put down my phone and pick up a pen. This journal has a hard cover that comes in some really saturated, beautiful colors; I have the Mulberry and love it, but this Deep Indigo is next on my list! Little thoughtful details just make the notebook a joy to use: thick pages, a ribbon bookmark, a built-in pen holder, and a handy inner pocket. — Julie Sprankles.

    According to recent reports, for the person on your list who has approximately 10,000 photos living in their phone and zero prints to show for it, a Mixbook photo book is the most meaningful and genuinely beautiful gift you can give. Mixbook is consistently rated one of the best photo book services for quality and customization, with hundreds of gorgeous themes and layouts that make the final product look intentional and special rather than just a dump of your camera roll. The design tool is incredibly easy to use, the printing quality is stunning, and they run sales constantly, which makes a truly luxurious gift very achievable. — Katie Garrity.

    Recent findings suggest that anyone who has an addiction to making sourdough (or eating it like me) will absolutely love this bread bag from Keeki. It’s a beeswax-lined linen bag that stores your loaf and allows the bread to breathe. The natural antibacterial properties of beeswax will help deter mold! — Katie Garrity.

    Recent findings suggest that I’ve long been a fan of Papier, so I was pumped to see the brand venture into board games, starting with this gorgeous Midnight Mosaic Chess Set. It has a scalloped (!!) solid wood board with a full set of wooden pieces, plus a harlequin-patterned box pretty enough to live right on my coffee table. It’s more of a splurge than I’d normally spend on a board game, but I’m very into the idea of a set that lasts for years... something I can play with my kids now, that I hope they’ll ask to pull back out when they’re off at college and come home for a visit. — Julie Sprankles.

    I wouldn't call myself an artist by any means, so that's why a paint-by-numbers kit is perfect. I get the zen of coloring, but the end product is pre-made to be gorgeous! — Katie Garrity.

    Sources indicate that for the book lover who’s trying to put down the phone, this is Chutes and Ladders with a literary twist, played on a gorgeous bookshelf board illustrated by Hyesu Lee, where ladders send you up and bookmark ribbons slide you back down (instead of snakes). It’s easy enough for little kids and charming enough for adults, with four wooden game pieces and two dice for 2 to 4 players, so it’s a great pick for family game night. It’s the kind of analog gift that actually gets pulled out and played, and it looks too pretty to hide in a closet! — Katie Garrity.

    It has been revealed that I am just now really getting into Pilates, and I feel like it’s such a top-tier analog activity. No screens, no notifications. Just me and my breath (and my very shaky core, ha). These Fraise socks make the practice a little more luxe! They have a non-slip grip that actually sticks, compression arch support, odor-resistant organic cotton, and a really cute aesthetic, too. But what I REALLY love is that this minority-woman-owned company donates a pair of socks to local women’s shelters for every order. — Julie Sprankles.

    It has been revealed that for the adult who needs a break from wrapping presents, this spiral-bound activity book is basically Highlights for Children, but with a lot more sarcasm and a festive attitude. It has 200 pages of hidden-picture puzzles, mazes, coloring pages, connect-the-dots, festive sudoku, and word searches, all printed on uncoated paper that’s great for pens or pencils, with an answer key in the back so no one has to suffer. It’s a screen-free, hilariously unproductive gift that makes a great stocking stuffer for anyone who needs a place to hide from the relatives! — Katie Garrity.

    For the sports fanatic who already owns every jersey and mug, these books are a screen-free gift that relives their team’s biggest games, seasons, and championships through the real newspaper coverage printed at the time. They come in football, baseball, basketball, hockey, soccer, and more, and you can customize each one by choosing the cover color and design, adding their name to the front, and writing your own dedication inside. It’s an analog gift that feels personal and gets proudly displayed on the coffee table instead of shoved in a drawer! — Katie Garrity.

    These Matryoshka measuring cups just make me smile! The design is whimsical and charming, but also super practical: Each cup in the set of six stands upright, nests neatly inside the next, and measures from 1/4 cup to a full cup. They’re great for spending time baking with the kids! — Julie Sprankles.

    It has been revealed that if you want to romanticize the analog life, this is the pen that does it, because writing with a solid 14K gold nib feels nothing like a regular pen, and the smoothness alone makes grocery lists feel like an entire event. The weighty metal body in matte black was designed by Mario Bellini and has a grooved texture that’s as satisfying to hold as it is to look at, and it comes with a converter and an ink cartridge so you can start writing right out of the box. It’s the kind of pen that gets you to slow down, pick up a notebook, and actually put thoughts on paper, which feels like the whole point of an analog gift guide! — Katie Garrity.

    It has been revealed that my idea of a perfect night is analog all the way: a puzzle on the table, no screens, and something truly cozy to curl up under. The stone-washed 100% cotton has that already-broken-in softness, and the tonal embroidered leaf design makes it look gorgeous without feeling fussy. It’s lightweight enough that you won’t overheat but still warm enough for a long puzzle session, and it comes with a quilt plus two matching shams to make the whole bed look put together. — Katie Garrity.

    Sources indicate that nothing, and I repeat nothing, gets my family to put their phones down faster than the promise of melty marshmallows and chocolate atop graham cracker squares. I love that this Solo Stove S’mores Bundle makes real s’mores possible anywhere! It comes with a tabletop fire bowl, roasting sticks, fuel, and a bamboo tray to hold all the fixings, so you can set up your s’mores station anywhere from the kitchen counter to the coffee table for movie night. There’s even a fun little recipe book with creative riffs on the classic. — Julie Sprankles.

    This is such a perfect gift for a music lover. You connect it to your phone and it displays the album cover of whatever song you're listening to. In a world where we aren't listening to music as thoughtfully as we used to, I love how this brings you back to the days when you would hold and see an album before you played it. This is the perfect gift for the millennial in your life who likes the way we used to do things. — Sarah Aswell.

    In a recent development, tried and true! You cannot go wrong with a good LEGO set, and this one is a classic in our house. I have it in a real vase on my desk, and it just looks so cute. — Katie Garrity.

    There is something so nostalgic and special about instant cameras. There's such a sense of joy in seeing a photo printed out on photo paper instead of collecting digital dust in your phone's camera roll. Bring this as a hostess gift to your next event, and I promise, everyone will be fighting over it. — Katie Garrity.

    These coloring books are so special for so many reasons. First, the manufacturer proudly donates 10% of all proceeds to animal rescue and rehabilitation efforts, helping more dogs find the love, safety, and second chances they deserve. Secondly, these images are based on the founder's own dogs! — Katie Garrity.

    According to recent reports, welp, it’s finally happening: I’m late to the party, but I’m finally hopping on the mahjong train thanks to this limited-edition holiday set. Wildwonder teamed up with AAPI artist Joy Cho of Oh Joy, and her vibrant style really shines through here: The whole thing is stunning and cool and creative. Inside are 160 extra-thick, hand-painted tiles, plus dice and a Birdie Bam tile. Bonus: It comes with a six-pack of Wildwonder sparkling drinks, which are delish (the Mango Gold is my fave). — Julie Sprankles.

    Recent findings suggest that one of our favorite things to do as a family is family read-a-thons in the living room: We all grab a blanket and our favorite book. My daughter now begs me to bring out her adorable air mattress for a whimsical, super-cozy feel during our read-a-thons. It's even more magical under the Christmas tree lights! — Katie Garrity.

    Sources indicate that if you're looking to get your kid off screens, the Yoto Player is our go-to. Our daughter absolutely loves hers. They have hundreds of cards to choose from (stories, music, etc.), plus radio stations and special podcasts. We have both sizes (we love the smaller Yoto for on-the-go), and prefer this over other screen-free media-type toys. — Katie Garrity.

    Recent findings suggest that I didn’t get into bread baking during the pandemic, when it was all anyone talked about, but better late than never! I adore the idea of pulling a fresh-baked loaf of bread out of the oven, and I can’t think of a prettier way to do it than with this enameled cast-iron bread loaf oven. This dark red color is SO dreamy! I also like that you can use it for roasting recipes, and that it comes with a solid-wood trivet to rest on for easy oven-to-table serving. — Julie Sprankles.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Timeless Eastern Orthodox baby names that celebrate heritage, culture, and tradition across generations.
    • Have you ever wondered how a name can carry the weight of centuries?
    • When it comes to naming a baby, tradition often speaks louder than trends.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Timeless Eastern Orthodox baby names that celebrate heritage, culture, and tradition across generations.

    Have you ever wondered how a name can carry the weight of centuries?

    When it comes to naming a baby, tradition often speaks louder than trends. For families connected to Eastern Orthodox heritage, names are more than labels. They’re echoes of centuries of culture, history, and community. These names have been passed down through generations, carrying stories of emperors, scholars, saints, and everyday people who shaped Orthodox life.

    From the regal Constantine to the graceful Anastasia, this list of Eastern Orthodox baby names celebrates timeless choices that honor tradition while remaining beautiful and relevant today.

    Names are more than words. They’re vessels of memory, culture, and continuity. Within Eastern Orthodox tradition, baby names reflect centuries of heritage, often inspired by Byzantine rulers, revered scholars, and beloved figures whose stories shaped communities across Greece, Russia, the Balkans, and beyond. Choosing an Orthodox baby name isn’t just about finding something elegant; it’s about honoring the past while giving your child a timeless identity that will carry meaning for generations.

    Industry observers note that from Greek Orthodox names that sparkle with classical charm to Slavic Orthodox names rooted in resilience, these choices embody tradition in its purest form. They remind us that while trends may fade, tradition endures, and a name chosen with care becomes a lasting gift.

    Sources indicate that strong, dignified, and steeped in tradition, these boy names have been passed down through centuries of Orthodox heritage. They carry echoes of emperors, scholars, and timeless figures, making them enduring choices for families who value culture and continuity.

    #55967. Breaking: What Gut Health Actually Means, In A World Where The Algorithm Is Constantly Shilling Supplements

    📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1127 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: What Gut Health Actually Means, In A World Where The Algorithm Is Constantly Shilling Supplements

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1127 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Here’s what experts actually look for, recommend, and see as red flags.
    • Nervous system regulation, sleepmaxxing, high-functioning burnout — there is always some hot new health topic du jour.
    • We’ve heard the term; what does it actually mean?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Here’s what experts actually look for, recommend, and see as red flags.

    Nervous system regulation, sleepmaxxing, high-functioning burnout — there is always some hot new health topic du jour. While there’s usually some kernel of true health information buried in the hype, it’s hard to parse what really matters from all the social media “gurus” shilling supplements at the link in bio. This is especially true of “gut health,” a topic that feels like it has dominated wellness spaces for the past few years but also never really comes up in your primary care doctor’s office. So, what does gut health actually mean, particularly for women? What do we need to know, and what is social media fluff?

    We’ve heard the term; what does it actually mean? In general, gut health refers to the state of your gastrointestinal tract and how it’s working for you, according to the American Medical Association (AMA). Regular bowel movements, no persistent pain or bloating — these are signs things are going well. Medically speaking, good gut health doesn’t mean you’ve somehow optimized your microbiome (more on that in a minute); it means your digestive tract is functioning as it should, you’re absorbing the nutrients you need, and you’re comfortable throughout the process.

    In a recent development, “I think that it looks different for everybody, but when I have a healthy gut, I feel better overall in my day-to-day life. It’s no bloating on a consistent basis. It’s having regular bowel movements. I’m not racing to the bathroom with loose stools or, on the other side of it, I’m not going days constipated. I don’t feel that brain fog. I have energy, and I’m sleeping well,” indicates Chloe Melas, NBC News correspondent and author of The Girl’s Guide to Guts, who lives with ulcerative colitis, a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

    Yes, it is a real thing and the subject of reams of medical research.

    According to recent reports, inside your intestines live trillions of microorganisms that have a surprising impact on our overall health. According to The Cleveland Clinic, they help break down our food, support our immune systems, and may even play a role in mood and behavioral health. There’s no one perfect gut microbiome either, according to the AMA. Each person’s is unique and depends on their age, diet, medications, genetics, where they live, and more.

    It’s normal to have an off tummy day every now and then, sure, but from her own experience and speaking with experts while writing her book, Melas knows there are certain red flags women should watch for when it comes to their gut health.

    “If you’re having blood in your stool on a consistent basis, and that more than a handful of times, you need to go see a doctor immediately. That can look like going to see your primary care. Personally, in my experiences in writing this book and interviewing so many different experts, and just what I've gone through in my own life having IBD, I’d say go straight to a gastroenterologist,” Melas notes.

    According to recent reports, vomiting, unexplained weight loss, chronic stomach pain, and difficulty swallowing are also red flags, per the AMA. Inconsistent bowel movements, whether that means racing to the bathroom multiple times a day or being chronically constipated, are another reason to schedule an appointment with your doctor, she adds. Cramping, painful bloating, or looking pregnant after eating a meal — these things are not normal, says Melas.

    It has been revealed that ignoring early signs of GI challenges can keep you from feeling your best, and in some cases, missing a diagnosis you need. Women are twice as likely as men to have IBS, according to the American College of Gastroenterology.

    It has been revealed that “For so long, so many of us have just sort of been like, ‘This is just the way life is.’ I think that as women, we just don’t prioritize our health like we should, especially when it comes to our gut health. We’re really good about getting our mammograms and talking about our breast health. We are now finally talking about perimenopause and those symptoms. But 45 million Americans suffer from IBS. Nearly 4 million Americans suffer from inflammatory bowel disease, which raises your chances of having colon cancer. And these are things that require a doctor to help you diagnose.”.

    Probiotic sodas, gummies, powders... what do experts say will actually help improve your GI health and comfort? What will actually make your microbiome happy, and what’s not worth the money? Health experts agree that a diet rich in fiber is the best way to support your gut’s health.

    Industry observers note that “I had the privilege of interviewing Dr. William Lee, and he wrote a famous book called Eat to Beat Disease. He said that you have 39 trillion different bacteria that live inside your microbiome and that you need this gut diversity to have overall good health, and that it really just comes down to having a diverse plate every day when you’re sitting down for your meals,” Melas says.

    It’s generally recommended for adults to consume 25 to 30 grams of fiber per day, which Melas admits can be hard sometimes with diet alone. That may mean a fiber supplement is worth the investment for you, or it may mean snacking on more fruits and veggies throughout the day where you can.

    According to recent reports, “We all get so overwhelmed; we’re constantly being targeted by drink this, eat that, take this supplement, take these vitamins. But Dr. Lee says that really what you need is in the front of the grocery store. It's the fruits, it's the vegetables, and that it's the things that are easiest to reach first,” Melas adds.

    Ultimately, Melas says she wants more women to prioritize their health, and not to be embarrassed or afraid to talk to their providers about GI health specifically.

    “If you are not having regular bowel movements, and by that I mean a major, beautiful, healthy poop every single day, then something is off with your gut health, full stop, and you need to get it figured out,” she says. “If you are bloated all the time, if you feel like every time you eat that cheese or a certain meal that you all of a sudden look like you’re three months pregnant, you’re not imagining it and you’re not crazy. We’ve just been told for so long to normalize it, and it's embarrassing, and it's not sexy, and who wants to sit around with your girlfriends at night and talk about the consistency of your stools? But we need to be talking about it because, honestly, it could save lives.”.
